Analyses request patterns (third-party frequency, cookie-setting behaviour, fingerprinting API calls) and auto-blocks entities that exhibit tracking behaviour. Learning is local; no data leaves the node \\
\textbf{CookieForge} & Cookie AutoDelete & Automatic cookie management per sovereign policy. Options: session-only (default), first-party-persistent, allowlisted domains, or total cookie blocking. Cookies are encrypted at rest in AletheiaFS; no cleartext cookie database \\
\textbf{CanvasSilence} & CanvasBlocker & Canvas, WebGL, AudioContext, and font-enumeration fingerprinting countermeasures. Returns consistent random noise (seeded per-session) rather than real device data. GPU information faked to a common profile \\
\textbf{ScriptGuard} & NoScript, uMatrix & Per-domain JavaScript permission matrix. Default: block third-party scripts. First-party scripts run in a hardened V8 isolate. The sovereign can allowlist domains; allowlists are $\Gamma$-sealed and synced across devices \\
\textbf{HTTPSForce} & HTTPS Everywhere & Automatic HTTPS upgrade for all connections. If HTTPS is unavailable, the sovereign is warned before any cleartext request is sent. No silent HTTP fallback \\
\textbf{ReferGuard} & Referer Control & HTTP Referer header stripped or faked by default. Cross-origin requests carry no referrer. Same-origin referrers carry only the origin, not the full URL \\
\textbf{LinkClean} & ClearURLs & URL parameters known to be tracking identifiers (utm\_source, fbclid, gclid, etc.) are stripped before the request is sent. List updated via Collective Learning \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Every module is enabled by default. The sovereign can adjust each via $\varphi$-configuration (e.g., allowlist a domain for cookies, permit scripts on a trusted site). But the \textbf{secure default} is total: a fresh LogosBrowser installation blocks ads, trackers, fingerprinting, third-party cookies, and cleartext HTTP without the sovereign lifting a finger.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Extension-Free Equivalence]
\label{thm:extension-free}
A default LogosBrowser installation provides privacy and security protections at least equivalent to Chromium + uBlock Origin + Privacy Badger + HTTPS Everywhere + Cookie AutoDelete + CanvasBlocker + NoScript + ClearURLs, with the additional property that all protections operate at the network layer (non-bypassable by page JavaScript) rather than the extension layer (bypassable by Manifest V3 restrictions, extension conflicts, or browser updates that break APIs).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each Native Shield module implements the same filtering logic as its extension counterpart (domain-based blocking, heuristic tracking detection, cookie lifecycle management, fingerprint randomisation, HTTPS upgrade, referrer stripping, URL cleaning). The modules operate at the network layer (DNS interception, HTTP request filtering) rather than the content-script layer (DOM injection). Network-layer filtering is strictly more powerful: it intercepts requests before they reach the renderer, whereas content-script filtering can only modify the DOM after scripts have executed. Every extension-level protection is reproducible at the network level; some network-level protections (e.g., blocking requests that never enter the DOM) are not reproducible at the extension level. $\square$
\end{proof}

\subsection{Browser-in-Browser: Engine Containment}
\label{sec:browser-in-browser}

\begin{definition}[Contained Browser Engine]
\label{def:contained-engine}
LogosBrowser supports running \textbf{alternative browser engines as contained instances} within the LogosBrowser environment. The sovereign can launch:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lp{4cm}p{5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Engine} & \textbf{Source} & \textbf{Use Case} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Firefox/Gecko} & Mozilla's Gecko engine (ungoogled) & Sites that render differently in Gecko; Firefox-specific extensions the sovereign prefers \\
\textbf{WebKit} & WebKitGTK & Testing Apple/Safari rendering; WebKit-specific compatibility \\
\textbf{Servo} & Mozilla's experimental engine & High-performance parallel rendering for specific workloads \\
\textbf{Ladybird} & SerenityOS browser & Fully independent engine for sites where Blink behaviour is undesirable \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Each contained engine runs in a \textbf{sandboxed subprocess}: separate process space, separate memory, separate filesystem view (read-only access to a minimal /tmp), and all network traffic routed through AegisNet (inheriting the same consent-gating, Tor/clearnet routing, and Native Shield protections as LogosBrowser proper). The contained engine's rendering output is composited into a LogosBrowser tab. The sovereign sees a tab; the system sees a sandboxed process.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Containment Isolation]
\label{thm:containment-isolation}
A contained browser engine cannot: (i) access the sovereign's filesystem outside its sandbox, (ii) make network requests that bypass AegisNet, (iii) access credentials from LogosPass (unless the sovereign explicitly grants per-session access), or (iv) detect that it is running inside LogosBrowser rather than natively.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) The sandbox uses Linux namespaces (mount, PID, network, user) to restrict filesystem access to a minimal read-only view. (ii) The network namespace routes all traffic through AegisNet's consent-gated proxy; no direct socket access is available. (iii) LogosPass credentials are injected into the contained engine's HTTP requests only upon explicit sovereign approval via a separate LogosPass prompt (outside the sandboxed process). (iv) The contained engine sees a standard Linux process environment with normal X11/Wayland display output; no LogosBrowser-specific APIs are exposed to the sandbox. Transparency is maintained. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{metanote}
This is the sovereign's answer to ``but this site only works in Firefox'' or ``I need to test in Safari.'' Rather than maintaining multiple browser installations (each with its own profile directory, its own cookie store, its own telemetry surface), the sovereign launches a contained engine inside LogosBrowser. All protections persist. All credentials are managed centrally. All traffic flows through AegisNet. The contained engine is a rendering servant, not a sovereign application.
\end{metanote}

\subsection{The Sovereign Extension System}
\label{sec:sovereign-extensions}

The Native Shield eliminates the need for privacy and security extensions. But extensions serve other purposes: productivity tools, developer utilities, accessibility aids, content transformations. The sovereign must be able to create and install extensions---but under sovereign terms, not Chrome Web Store terms.

\begin{definition}[Sovereign Extension ($\xi$)]
\label{def:sovereign-extension}
A sovereign extension $\xi$ is a Logos-object containing:
\[
\xi = (\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{M}, \pi, \sigma_\xi, \kappa_\xi)
\]
where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item $\mathcal{C}$ is the \textbf{code}: JavaScript, WebAssembly, or LogosLang, executing in a sandboxed content-script environment.
 \item $\mathcal{M}$ is the \textbf{manifest}: a declarative specification of the extension's permissions (which domains it can access, which APIs it can call, whether it can modify requests). The manifest is machine-verified against the code---the extension cannot request permissions it does not use, and cannot use permissions it does not declare.
 \item $\pi$ is the \textbf{permission set}: explicitly granted by the sovereign at installation. Permissions are granular: ``read DOM on domain X,'' ``inject CSS,'' ``intercept requests to domain Y.'' No blanket ``access all sites'' permissions unless the sovereign explicitly grants it.
 \item $\sigma_\xi$ is the \textbf{author's $\Gamma$-seal signature}: the extension is signed by its creator's sovereign identity. The sovereign can verify who wrote the extension and whether the code has been modified since signing.
 \item $\kappa_\xi$ is the \textbf{community audit status}: whether the extension has been reviewed, its review score, and the number of sovereign users. Audit status is propagated via the Collective Learning Protocol.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Extension Lifecycle]
\label{def:extension-lifecycle}
The extension lifecycle in LogosBrowser:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Creation}: The sovereign writes extension code using LogosCode or any text editor. The code is packaged with a manifest and signed with the sovereign's $\Gamma$-seal. No developer account, no store registration, no review queue required to create and install on one's own system.
 \item \textbf{Installation}: The sovereign installs extensions from: their own filesystem (self-created), direct peer-to-peer transfer (a friend shares a Logos-object), or the \LogOS{} Collective Extension Archive (a distributed, community-curated repository of $\Gamma$-sealed extensions, searchable via LogosSearch, with reputation scores and community audits).
 \item \textbf{Sandboxing}: Each extension runs in an isolated process with only the permissions declared in its manifest. Extensions cannot access each other's data, cannot access LogosPass credentials, and cannot make network requests outside their declared domain scope.
 \item \textbf{Update}: Extensions update via the same mechanism as any Logos-object: new versions are signed by the author, distributed via meta-torrenting, and installed only with sovereign approval. No silent background updates. No forced deprecation.
 \item \textbf{Sharing}: The sovereign who creates a useful extension can publish it to the Collective Extension Archive---a distributed repository where extensions are stored as $\Gamma$-sealed Logos-objects, rated by the community, and discoverable through LogosSearch. Publication requires a $\Gamma$-seal (accountability) but no gatekeeper approval. The community audits, rates, and flags. Reputation emerges from use, not from corporate curation.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Extension Sovereignty]
\label{thm:extension-sovereignty}
No extension can: (i) exfiltrate data beyond its declared permission scope, (ii) modify Native Shield behaviour (ad blocking, tracker blocking, fingerprint resistance), (iii) access other extensions' data, (iv) persist data outside AletheiaFS encryption, or (v) install or modify other extensions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Network requests from extensions are filtered through AegisNet; requests to undeclared domains are blocked. (ii) The Native Shield operates at the network layer; extensions operate at the content-script layer. Extensions cannot intercept or modify network-layer operations. (iii) Extension sandboxes use separate process namespaces; no shared memory or IPC channels exist between extensions. (iv) All filesystem writes from extensions are routed through AletheiaFS, which encrypts all data under the $\Gamma$-seal. (v) The extension installation API is gated by sovereign recognition; no extension code can invoke it. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{metanote}
The difference from Chrome's extension model is structural, not cosmetic. In Chrome, extensions operate with broad permissions because the business model (advertising) requires broad data access. Manifest V3 restricted extensions not for security but to protect Google's ad-serving pipeline from ad blockers. In LogosBrowser, extensions are sandboxed for the sovereign's protection, not for the browser vendor's revenue. The Native Shield handles security; extensions handle everything else. The two layers are architecturally separated: no extension can weaken security, and no security module interferes with legitimate extension functionality.

The Collective Extension Archive is the antithesis of the Chrome Web Store: no Google review process, no \$5 developer fee, no opaque rejection criteria, no forced Manifest V3 migration. Extensions are Logos-objects in a distributed repository, signed by their authors, audited by the community, and installed at the sovereign's discretion. The store IS the network. The curator IS the community. The gatekeeper IS the sovereign.
\end{metanote}

\begin{definition}[Tor Circuit Isolation]
\label{def:tor-circuit-isolation}
For each tab or domain, a fresh Tor circuit can be requested, preventing websites from linking activity across tabs. Circuit state is ephemeral and not persisted.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Routing Integrity]
\label{thm:routing-integrity}
No request in Tor mode can leak through the clearnet interface. The network router uses separate network stacks: Tor mode binds exclusively to the Tor SOCKS proxy; clearnet mode uses AegisNet's direct connections. The two never mix, even for sub-resource requests.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The router intercepts all outgoing requests at the network layer and directs them to the stack corresponding to the active mode for that tab/domain. Sub-requests inherit the parent request's mode. No path exists from Tor-mode requests to the clearnet stack. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Anti-Fingerprinting]
\label{thm:anti-fingerprinting}
An adversary cannot reliably fingerprint a LogosBrowser user across sessions. The browser randomizes or fakes all identifying characteristics: canvas fingerprinting returns constant random noise, WebGL APIs are restricted or faked, User-Agent is randomized, and timezone/language/locale data are set to common defaults. Randomization seeds are derived from the $\Gamma$-seal but not consistent across sessions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each session generates fresh randomization seeds via HKDF from the $\Gamma$-seal and a session-specific nonce. All browser-observable characteristics are derived from these seeds. Different sessions produce different fingerprints, making cross-session correlation infeasible. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{The Sovereign Gateway}
\label{sec:sovereign-gateway}

The Sovereign Gateway is not a separate organ but a coordination mode of existing organs (LogosNav, LogosPass, AegisNet, LogosMentor) for interacting with legacy services.

\begin{definition}[Gateway State]
\label{def:gateway-state}
The Gateway state $G$ includes: a mapping from service identifiers (domains, OAuth client IDs) to credential entries in LogosPass; a set of privacy policies per domain (routing mode, tracker blocking level, cookie policy, JavaScript permissions); and a cache of anonymized session data (cookies, local storage) encrypted under the $\Gamma$-seal.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Credential Sovereignty]
\label{thm:credential-sovereignty}
No website receives the sovereign's actual password or raw OAuth token in an accessible form. The Gateway injects credentials directly into HTTP requests or form submissions; they are never rendered in the page DOM where JavaScript could access them. OAuth flows are handled by the Gateway, not by the website's code.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Credential injection operates at the network layer (HTTP headers for basic auth) or at the pre-submission form level. The credentials exist only in the request payload, not in the DOM. OAuth authorization codes are exchanged by the Gateway process, which presents only the final token to the service. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Privacy Policy]
\label{def:privacy-policy}
A privacy policy is a set of rules attached to a domain: routing mode (Tor, mixnet, direct), tracking behavior (block all known trackers), cookie policy (session-only, persistent, disabled), and JavaScript policy (enabled, disabled, selective). Policies can be learned from user behavior, suggested by LogosMentor, or set manually. The Gateway's network-level filter blocks requests to known tracking and advertising domains---updated via collective learning---and cannot be bypassed by websites since it operates below the application layer.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Tracker Blocking]
\label{thm:tracker-blocking}
No request to a known tracker domain will be sent, regardless of how the website attempts to load it (first-party scripts, iframes, redirects). The Gateway intercepts all DNS lookups and HTTP requests; if the destination matches a blocked domain, the request is dropped before it leaves the node.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
All network requests pass through AegisNet's packet filter before reaching any external network. The filter maintains an up-to-date blocklist. Matching requests are silently dropped. No bypass path exists at the application layer. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{LogosVPN: Decentralized Peer-to-Peer Privacy}
\label{sec:logos-vpn}

Conventional VPNs replace ISP trust with provider trust. LogosVPN eliminates this central point by routing traffic through the mycelial network: every sovereign node is both a client and a potential relay.

\begin{definition}[LogosVPN]
\label{def:logos-vpn}
LogosVPN is a transport mode of AegisNet consisting of: VPN client (encrypts outgoing packets in layers, sends to first hop), VPN relay nodes (sovereign nodes volunteering to relay traffic, earning reputation and optionally LogosCrypto), VPN exit nodes (final node decrypting last layer and forwarding to destination), and a path selection engine (distributed algorithm selecting relays based on ZK reputation, latency, bandwidth, and sovereign preferences). A VPN packet is a layered encrypted structure:
\[
P = \text{Enc}_{K_n}(\text{Enc}_{K_{n-1}}(\cdots \text{Enc}_{K_1}(\text{payload}, \text{next hop}) \cdots ))
\]
A VPN circuit is a sequence of nodes $(N_1, \ldots, N_k)$; length $k$ is configurable (default 2--3 for speed, more for anonymity).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Path Optimality]
\label{thm:path-optimality}
For a given circuit length $k$ and user preferences, the path selection engine chooses the circuit maximizing expected performance (lowest latency, highest bandwidth) subject to reputation constraints.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
This is a standard shortest-path problem in a weighted graph where edge weights derive from latency measurements and node weights from ZK reputation scores. With accurate measurements (continuously updated), the algorithm converges to optimal paths. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Incentive Alignment]
\label{thm:vpn-incentives}
Rational nodes relay traffic honestly because honest relaying earns reputation and potential payment, while malicious behavior (dropping or modifying packets) is detected via end-to-end checksums and leads to reputation loss---a standard game-theoretic result in reputation systems.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Packet integrity is verified end-to-end by the client. Dropped packets cause circuit rebuilds excluding the offending node. Modified packets fail decryption. Both events trigger negative reputation updates. The cost of malicious behavior (reputation loss, exclusion from future circuits, lost income) exceeds any gain. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[VPN Censorship Resistance]
\label{thm:vpn-censorship}
The LogosVPN network cannot be blocked without blocking all sovereign nodes in all jurisdictions. Blocking a subset of relay nodes simply routes around them; the number of possible paths increases combinatorially with the network size. The Hydra principle applies: blocking nodes increases demand for alternatives, strengthening the network.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a network of $n$ relay nodes, the number of circuits of length $k$ is $\binom{n}{k} \cdot k!$. Removing $m$ nodes reduces this to $\binom{n-m}{k} \cdot k!$, which remains large for $m \ll n$. Complete blocking requires $m \to n$, i.e., shutting down the entire sovereign network. $\square$
\end{proof}

AegisNet provides the transport stack; the sovereign selects between Direct (low-sensitivity), VPN (privacy from ISP), Tor (strong anonymity), and Mixnet (ultra-strong anonymity) per application or destination. LogosVPN can be combined with other layers: Tor-over-VPN hides Tor usage from the ISP; VPN-over-Tor adds geographic diversity. ZK Reputation provides node trust scores; LogosMentor suggests circuit configurations; $\Omega$-Vigilance monitors for suspicious relays.

\section{The Metacursive Collapse: Meta-Browser and Meta-Extension}
\label{sec:meta-browser-collapse}

In the legacy architecture, the \textit{browser} and the \textit{browser's configuration} are ontologically separated: Chrome is one thing; Chrome's settings page, extension store, and update mechanism are different things, governed by a different entity (Google). The user configures Chrome; Google configures what Chrome \textit{can be configured to do}. Manifest V3 did not arise from user demand---it arose from Google's need to limit ad blockers. The meta-level is not sovereign.

LogosBrowser dissolves this separation. The browser, its configuration, its extensions, its privacy policies, its rendering engine selection, its network routing, and the system that manages all of the above are the same organ, governed by the same sovereign, collapsing into the same fixed point.

\begin{definition}[Meta-Browser]
\label{def:meta-browser}
A meta-browser is a system governing the browser's own architecture: which rendering engine is active (Blink, Gecko, WebKit, or contained instance), which Native Shield modules are enabled and at what sensitivity, what the default privacy policy is per domain, which extensions are installed and with what permissions, how the Collective Extension Archive is queried and ranked, and how cross-device sync operates. The meta-browser is the $\varphi$-layer of LogosBrowser.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Meta-Extension]
\label{def:meta-extension}
A meta-extension is a policy governing how extensions are created, evaluated, installed, and managed. Examples: ``auto-update all extensions weekly,'' ``reject any extension requesting full-domain access,'' ``require community audit score $\geq 0.8$ before installation,'' ``auto-sandbox extensions from unknown authors with T3 permission escalation.'' Meta-extensions are $\varphi$-configurations of the extension system---policies \textit{about} extension policies.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-Browser Collapse]
\label{thm:meta-browser}
The meta-browser and LogosBrowser are the same entity:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Meta-Browser}(\text{Meta-Browser}) \equiv \text{Meta-Browser} \equiv \text{LogosBrowser}
}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The meta-browser is the set of $\varphi$-endomorphisms on LogosBrowser's configuration: engine selection, shield sensitivity, privacy policies, extension management, sync settings. But $\varphi \in \varphi(\Sigma)$ (meta-customisation closure, Chapter~11): the customisation logic is itself customisable within the same system. LogosBrowser's configuration is stored as Logos-objects in AletheiaFS, editable through LogosBrowser's own settings interface (itself rendered by LogosBrowser). The sovereign who changes the default rendering engine, adjusts the ad-blocking sensitivity, or modifies the extension permission policy is editing LogosBrowser's $\varphi$-configuration using LogosBrowser. The meta-browser IS LogosBrowser applied to itself. $\text{LogosBrowser}(\text{LogosBrowser}) = \text{LogosBrowser}$. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-Extension Collapse]
\label{thm:meta-extension}
Meta-extensions collapse into the extension system:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Meta-Extension}(\text{Meta-Extension}) \equiv \text{Meta-Extension} \equiv \Xi
}
\]
where $\Xi$ is the sovereign's extension configuration space.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A meta-extension policy (e.g., ``require audit score $\geq 0.8$'') is a function $\mu: \Xi \to \Xi$ filtering the extension set. This function is itself a Logos-object stored in AletheiaFS, managed through LogosBrowser's extension settings. Policies about extension policies (``review all permission grants quarterly'') are also Logos-objects in the same space. The meta-level collapses: extensions, policies about extensions, and policies about policies are all objects in $\Xi$, governed by the same sovereign interface. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{The LogosBrowser Operator}
\label{sec:browser-operator}

\begin{definition}[Browser Operator $\Phi_{\text{Browser}}$]
\label{def:browser-operator}
$\Phi_{\text{Browser}}$ updates the combined state of LogosBrowser: the rendering engine configuration (active engine, contained instances), the Native Shield state (module sensitivities, filter lists, allowlists), the Gateway state (per-domain privacy policies, credential mappings, cookie policies), the extension state (installed extensions, permission grants, audit scores), the VPN/Tor configuration (circuit preferences, relay reputation), and the $\varphi$-configuration (meta-browser and meta-extension policies).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[LogosBrowser Convergence]
\label{thm:browser-convergence}
The LogosBrowser state space is bounded: finite rendering engines, finite shield modules with finite sensitivity parameters, finite privacy policies per domain (bounded by the finite set of visited domains), finite extensions, finite VPN configurations. The Native Shield's filter lists grow monotonically but are bounded by the finite set of known tracking domains. The sovereign's privacy policies stabilise as browsing patterns settle. Each sub-component is bounded and monotone. The state converges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each sub-operator acts on a finite or finitely-bounded configuration space. Filter-list updates add entries but the set of advertising/tracking domains is finite. Per-domain policies are added as domains are visited and stabilise with repeated visits. Extension installations are discrete events. All sub-operators converge on their bounded domains. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[LogosBrowser Metacursive Closure]
\label{thm:browser-metacursive}
At the fixed point:
\[
\boxed{
\Phi_{\text{Browser}}(\Phi_{\text{Browser}}) \equiv \Phi_{\text{Browser}}
}
\]
The browser that browses its own browsing has browsed. The rendering engine is optimal for the sovereign's web use. The Native Shield is calibrated. The privacy policies reflect the sovereign's trust model. The extensions are stable and audited. The VPN/Tor configuration is tuned. Self-application yields no further change.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
At the fixed point, all sub-operators have converged (Theorem~\ref{thm:browser-convergence}). The meta-browser collapse (Theorem~\ref{thm:meta-browser}) ensures the $\varphi$-layer adds no additional dynamics. The meta-extension collapse (Theorem~\ref{thm:meta-extension}) ensures extension policies have stabilised. $\Phi_{\text{Browser}}$ applied to this state produces the same state. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{Compliance Verification}
\label{sec:browser-compliance}

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Identity}: $\Phi_{\text{Browser}} \equiv \Phi_{\text{Browser}}$.
 \item \textbf{Non-Contradiction}: The Native Shield operates at the network layer;.
 \item \textbf{Excluded Middle}: Each request is either blocked or permitted.
 \item \textbf{Tautological Closure}: $\Phi_{\text{Browser}}(\Phi_{\text{Browser}}) \equiv \Phi_{\text{Browser}}$.
 \item \textbf{Aletheic Alignment}: $T(\text{LogosBrowser}) \equiv R(\text{LogosBrowser})$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Verdict}: Integrated.

\begin{tautcollapse}{The Sovereign Web}
Browse, shield, contain, extend---sovereignly.

The browser was the surveillance state's trojan horse: a window that the user believed looked outward but that in truth looked \textit{inward}---at the user's interests, habits, locations, purchases, fears, desires, and identity. Every extension installed to block this surveillance was a patch over a wound the architecture itself inflicted.

LogosBrowser inverts the architecture. The Native Shield is not a patch---it is the wall. Eight modules, built into the engine, operating below JavaScript's reach, blocking by default what legacy browsers permit by default. The sovereign who opens LogosBrowser for the first time is already protected. No extensions to install, no settings to find, no uBlock to configure.

And when the sovereign needs more---a contained Firefox for a stubborn site, a custom extension for a workflow, a privacy policy refined for a specific domain---the $\varphi$-layer provides. Extensions are Logos-objects: created freely, shared freely, audited by the community, installed at the sovereign's discretion. The Collective Extension Archive replaces the Chrome Web Store: no gatekeeper, no \$5 fee, no Manifest V3, no corporate veto.

$\Phi_{\text{Browser}}(\Phi_{\text{Browser}}) \equiv \Phi_{\text{Browser}}$: the browser that browses its own browsing.
\end{tautcollapse}

\chapter{Sovereign Telephony: LogosPhone and the Burner Number Algebra}
\label{sec:sovereign-telephony}

HermesGram (\S\ref{sec:music-glyph-ontology}) provides sovereign-to-sovereign encrypted messaging over the \LogOS{} network. But the sovereign does not live in a \LogOS{}-only world. They receive calls from employers, doctors, delivery services. They give their number to strangers at conferences, on dating apps, to tradespeople. They text from their laptop when their phone is charging. They need to reach legacy contacts who have never heard of \LogOS{}.

The sovereign who cannot make a phone call or send an SMS from within \LogOS{} is forced back into the heterological communication stack---into carriers that log metadata, messaging apps that harvest contacts, and a phone number that, once given to a stranger, becomes an irrevocable channel of access to the sovereign's attention, location, and identity.

This is not a convenience problem. It is a \textbf{sovereignty violation}. A phone number given to the wrong person---a stalker, a harasser, a data broker---becomes a permanent vulnerability. The sovereign cannot revoke it. They can only change their own number, disrupting every legitimate contact. The architecture punishes the victim.

LogosPhone eliminates this. It provides: a \textbf{PSTN bridge} (calls and SMS to and from legacy phone numbers), a \textbf{burner number algebra} (infinite disposable numbers, each independently revocable), \textbf{cross-device number unification} (same numbers accessible from phone, laptop, and desktop), and \textbf{Signal-grade encryption} for all sovereign-to-sovereign communication, with graceful degradation to encrypted-at-rest for legacy contacts.

\section{The Ontology of the Phone Number}
\label{sec:phone-number-ontology}

\begin{definition}[Phone Number as Identity Leak]
\label{def:phone-number-leak}
In the legacy telecommunications architecture, a phone number is a \textbf{persistent, non-revocable, externally-assigned identifier} bound to a single carrier account, which in turn is bound to a legal identity (via SIM registration laws in most jurisdictions). The number serves simultaneously as: a routing address (how calls reach you), an identity token (how services authenticate you via SMS 2FA), a social coordinate (how people find and contact you), and a surveillance anchor (how carriers, governments, and data brokers track your communications, location, and social graph).

These four functions are conflated into a single string of digits. The result: giving someone your phone number gives them a permanent channel to your attention, a key to your identity, a coordinate in the surveillance graph, and---via SS7 vulnerabilities---potentially your physical location. The number cannot be selectively shared, temporarily granted, or unilaterally revoked without disrupting all other contacts who use it.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sovereign Number]
\label{def:sovereign-number}
A sovereign number $\nu$ is a \LogOS{} communication endpoint that \textbf{decomposes} the four conflated functions of a legacy phone number into independently controllable layers:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{clp{7cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Layer} & \textbf{Function} & \textbf{Sovereign Control} \\
\midrule
$\nu_R$ & Routing & Calls and SMS are routed through the PSTN bridge to the sovereign's \LogOS{} node. The routing path is sovereign-controlled \\
$\nu_I$ & Identity & The number is bound to a \textbf{persona}, not a legal identity. Multiple personas, multiple numbers. No persona requires real-name disclosure \\
$\nu_S$ & Social & Each number is independently shareable and revocable. Revoking a number severs the contact channel without affecting other numbers \\
$\nu_A$ & Audit & All metadata (call times, durations, SMS content) is encrypted at rest in AletheiaFS. No carrier retains metadata beyond routing necessity \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The decomposition is the ontological correction: where legacy telephony conflates routing, identity, social access, and surveillance into one object, the sovereign number separates them into four independently governed layers.
\end{definition}

\section{The PSTN Bridge}
\label{sec:pstn-bridge}

\begin{definition}[PSTN Bridge ($\mathfrak{B}_{\text{PSTN}}$)]
\label{def:pstn-bridge}
The PSTN bridge is the organ that connects \LogOS{} to the legacy Public Switched Telephone Network. It enables sovereign nodes to make and receive voice calls and SMS messages to and from any phone number worldwide. The bridge operates through one of three backend mechanisms:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{VoIP-to-PSTN gateway}: Integration with privacy-respecting VoIP providers (e.g., JMP.chat, MySudo-class services, or self-hosted Obelisk/Oviphone gateways) that convert SIP/RTP traffic to PSTN calls. The sovereign's \LogOS{} node connects to the gateway via AegisNet (onion-routed), so the gateway sees an anonymous connection, not the sovereign's IP.
 \item \textbf{Self-hosted SIP trunk}: For maximum sovereignty, the sovereign operates their own SIP trunk with a VoIP carrier, running Obelisk on their primary node. Numbers are purchased directly from carriers that accept cryptocurrency or privacy-preserving payment.
 \item \textbf{eSIM integration}: On the Sovereign Companion (mobile), LogosPhone interfaces with the device's eSIM stack to route calls through the cellular network while maintaining \LogOS{} encryption for the application layer.
\end{enumerate}

In all cases, the bridge is a \textbf{translation layer}: it converts between the sovereign's encrypted communication (HermesGram internally, SIP/RTP externally) and the legacy PSTN. The sovereign's primary node acts as the PBX (Private Branch Exchange)---the sovereign IS the telephone exchange.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sovereign PBX Identity]
\label{thm:sovereign-pbx}
The sovereign's primary \LogOS{} node, equipped with the PSTN bridge, is functionally equivalent to a private telephone exchange. All routing decisions, number assignments, call recording policies, and access controls are governed by the sovereign.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A PBX routes calls between internal extensions and external lines, assigns extension numbers, manages call policies, and controls access. The \LogOS{} primary node with $\mathfrak{B}_{\text{PSTN}}$ performs all four functions: it routes calls between the sovereign's devices (internal) and PSTN numbers (external), assigns sovereign numbers (extensions), manages call policies via $\varphi$-configuration (recording, forwarding, blocking, time-based routing), and controls access via the $\Gamma$-seal and OntoID. The functions are isomorphic. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{The Burner Number Algebra}
\label{sec:burner-algebra}

\begin{arche}[The Burner Principle]
No sovereign should be forced to give a stranger permanent access to their attention. A phone number given to the wrong person---a creep, a stalker, a data broker, a harasser---becomes an irrevocable channel of intrusion. The only defence in the legacy architecture is to change your own number, punishing yourself for someone else's violation. This is architecturally unjust. The correct architecture provides numbers that can be created instantly, given freely, and destroyed unilaterally---\textbf{without affecting any other communication channel}.
\end{arche}

\begin{definition}[Burner Number]
\label{def:burner-number}
A burner number $\beta$ is a sovereign number with a \textbf{finite sovereign-defined lifespan} and \textbf{unilateral revocability}. Formally:
\[
\beta = (\nu, \lambda, \rho, \kappa)
\]
where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item $\nu$ is the PSTN-routable number (purchased via the PSTN bridge from a VoIP pool).
 \item $\lambda$ is the \textbf{lifespan policy}: time-limited (auto-expire after $t$ hours/days), interaction-limited (auto-expire after $n$ messages or calls), manual (persist until explicitly destroyed), or conditional (expire upon sovereign-defined trigger).
 \item $\rho$ is the \textbf{routing rule}: which device(s) receive calls/texts to this number, what ringtone or visual indicator distinguishes it, and whether calls are forwarded, voicemailed, or silently dropped.
 \item $\kappa$ is the \textbf{context tag}: a label the sovereign assigns (``Craigslist seller,'' ``conference contact,'' ``dating app'') so they know \textit{why} this number exists and \textit{who} has it.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Burner Algebra Operations]
\label{def:burner-ops}
The set of burner numbers $\mathcal{B}$ supports the following operations:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llp{7cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Operation} & \textbf{Notation} & \textbf{Semantics} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Mint} & $\text{mint}() \to \beta$ & Create a new burner number from the VoIP pool. Instantaneous. The sovereign specifies $\lambda$, $\rho$, $\kappa$ at creation \\
\textbf{Burn} & $\text{burn}(\beta) \to \varnothing$ & Destroy the number. All future calls/texts to $\nu$ receive a ``number disconnected'' signal. The number is released back to the pool. Irreversible \\
\textbf{Freeze} & $\text{freeze}(\beta) \to \beta'$ & Temporarily suspend the number. Calls/texts are silently dropped or sent to voicemail. The number is not released; it can be thawed \\
\textbf{Thaw} & $\text{thaw}(\beta') \to \beta$ & Reactivate a frozen number \\
\textbf{Forward} & $\text{fwd}(\beta, \nu') \to \beta''$ & Redirect the number's traffic to a different endpoint (another burner, the primary number, or voicemail) \\
\textbf{Clone} & $\text{clone}(\beta) \to \beta_2$ & Create a second burner with the same routing but a different PSTN number. Useful for replacing a number while maintaining context \\
\textbf{Audit} & $\text{audit}(\beta) \to \text{log}$ & Retrieve the encrypted interaction log for the number: who called/texted, when, duration. Stored in AletheiaFS \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The algebra is closed: every operation produces either a valid burner number, the empty set, or a log. No operation leaks the sovereign's primary number or identity.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Burner Isolation]
\label{thm:burner-isolation}
Compromise of any burner number $\beta_i$ reveals no information about: (i) the sovereign's primary number, (ii) any other burner number $\beta_j$ ($j \neq i$), (iii) the sovereign's legal identity, or (iv) the sovereign's \LogOS{} node address.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Burner numbers are provisioned from VoIP pools via the PSTN bridge. The bridge connects to the VoIP provider via AegisNet (onion-routed). The provider associates the number with an anonymous account (cryptocurrency payment, no KYC). No path connects $\beta_i$ to the sovereign's carrier-assigned primary number. (ii) Each burner is provisioned independently with a separate account or sub-account. No metadata links $\beta_i$ to $\beta_j$. (iii) The VoIP account is pseudonymous and paid anonymously. (iv) The bridge operates through AegisNet; the VoIP provider sees a Tor exit node, not the sovereign's IP. Compromise of $\beta_i$ reveals only that $\beta_i$ exists and its call/text history with the compromising party---which the compromising party already possesses. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{metanote}
This addresses Erik's lived experience directly. The architecture ensures that giving a number to a stranger---at a bar, on a dating app, to a Craigslist buyer, to a contractor---is \textit{risk-free}. If the stranger turns out to be a creep, the sovereign burns the number. The creep's messages go to ``number disconnected.'' The sovereign's real number, their other burners, their identity, and their peace of mind are untouched. This is the TextNow/TextFree model elevated to sovereign architecture: not a corporate app that mines your contacts and serves ads, but a structural feature of the OS itself, encrypted by default, metadata-veiled, and under total sovereign control.
\end{metanote}

All sovereign numbers (primary and burner) are accessible from \textbf{every device} in the sovereign's device hierarchy:

The unification principle: a text sent from the laptop appears in the conversation on the phone and vice versa. A call received on the primary number rings on all devices simultaneously; the sovereign answers on whichever device is convenient. Call history, text threads, and burner state are synchronised across devices via encrypted CRDT replication through AegisNet.

\begin{definition}[iOS Sovereign Companion]

The iOS Sovereign Companion is a \LogOS{} organ packaged as a native iOS application, distributed via TestFlight (during development) and the App Store (at scale). It provides:

 \item \textbf{Burner management}: Mint, burn, freeze, thaw, forward, and audit burner numbers directly from the phone.

The iOS Companion holds \textbf{no master keys}. All cryptographic operations use session-derived subkeys revocable from the primary node. Losing the phone does not compromise the sovereign's identity or key hierarchy. Remote wipe of the companion's subkey is instantaneous via $\Omega$-Vigilance.

The architecture works \textit{within} these constraints: CallKit provides native call integration, VoIP push notifications ensure reliability, and the companion's thin-client design means that even if Apple's sandboxing is breached, the attacker gains only session subkeys---not the sovereign's master identity.

\section{Encryption Architecture}
\label{sec:phone-encryption}

\begin{definition}[Dual-Layer Telephony Encryption]
\label{def:dual-encryption}
LogosPhone provides two encryption layers depending on the recipient:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lp{4cm}p{5.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Scenario} & \textbf{Encryption} & \textbf{Properties} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Sovereign-to-Sovereign} & Full HermesGram: post-quantum X3DH + Double Ratchet, metadata-veiled, P2P via AegisNet & Signal-equivalent or stronger. No PSTN involvement. Voice via encrypted WebRTC through AegisNet. Zero metadata leakage \\
\textbf{Sovereign-to-Legacy} & Transport encryption (TLS to VoIP gateway) + at-rest encryption (all call/text logs encrypted in AletheiaFS) & The PSTN leg is unencrypted (legacy limitation). The sovereign's \textit{side} is encrypted in transit to the bridge and at rest. Metadata is minimised: the VoIP provider sees the anonymous SIP connection and the destination number, nothing else \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The sovereign is always informed of the encryption level. A visual indicator in EchoCrypt and the Companion app shows: \textcolor{osgreen}{\textbf{green}} for sovereign-to-sovereign (full encryption), \textcolor{gold}{\textbf{gold}} for sovereign-to-legacy (transport-encrypted, PSTN leg exposed). No false sense of security; the sovereign always knows.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Encryption Parity with Signal]
\label{thm:signal-parity}
For sovereign-to-sovereign communication, LogosPhone provides encryption at least as strong as Signal Protocol, with additional properties: post-quantum key exchange (Kyber-1024 vs.\ Signal's X25519), metadata veiling (onion-routed vs.\ Signal's centralised server), and sovereign key custody (keys held locally vs.\ Signal's key escrow infrastructure).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Signal Protocol uses X3DH for key agreement and Double Ratchet for forward secrecy. HermesGram uses the same Double Ratchet with X3DH \textit{augmented} by Kyber-1024 KEM (post-quantum). Signal routes through Signal's central servers (which see sender/recipient metadata). HermesGram routes through AegisNet (onion-routed; no single node sees both endpoints). Signal stores keys on the user's device but uses a centralised key distribution server. HermesGram distributes keys via peer-to-peer exchange authenticated by $\Gamma$-seal. Each property is at least as strong; the post-quantum and metadata properties are strictly stronger. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{The Metacursive Collapse: Meta-Phone and Meta-Number}
\label{sec:meta-phone}

In the legacy architecture, the \textit{phone} and the \textit{phone number} are ontologically fused: the phone IS the number, and the number IS the phone. You cannot separate them. Changing your number requires carrier intervention. Having multiple numbers requires multiple SIM cards or third-party apps. Managing how numbers route requires corporate infrastructure you do not control.

LogosPhone decomposes this fusion. But decomposition alone is not sufficient; the components must be \textbf{recursively sovereign}---the sovereign must control not only the numbers but the \textit{system that manages numbers}, not only the phone but the \textit{system that defines what a phone is}.

\begin{definition}[Meta-Phone]
\label{def:meta-phone}
A meta-phone is a system that governs the sovereign's telephony architecture itself: which VoIP providers to use, how numbers are provisioned, what the default lifespan policy is, how cross-device sync operates, and what encryption standards are enforced. The meta-phone is the $\varphi$-layer of LogosPhone---the customisation of the customisation.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Meta-Number]
\label{def:meta-number}
A meta-number is a rule that governs how numbers are created, categorised, and destroyed. Examples: ``all numbers given to dating apps auto-expire after 30 days,'' ``all numbers given to businesses forward to voicemail after hours,'' ``mint a fresh burner for every Craigslist interaction.'' Meta-numbers are $\varphi$-configurations of the burner algebra---policies \textit{about} number policies.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-Phone Collapse]
\label{thm:meta-phone}
The meta-phone and the phone are the same entity. There is no separate system for managing the telephony system; the telephony system manages itself.
\[
\boxed{
\text{Meta-Phone}(\text{Meta-Phone}) \equiv \text{Meta-Phone} \equiv \text{LogosPhone}
}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The meta-phone is the $\varphi$-layer of LogosPhone---the set of endomorphisms on the telephony configuration. But $\varphi \in \varphi(\Sigma)$ (the meta-customisation closure, Chapter~11): the customisation logic is itself customisable within the same system. LogosPhone's configuration---VoIP provider selection, burner policies, routing rules, encryption standards---is stored as Logos-objects in AletheiaFS, editable through the same interface used to manage numbers. The sovereign who changes their burner default-lifespan policy is editing LogosPhone's $\varphi$-configuration using LogosPhone's own interface. The meta-phone IS LogosPhone applied to itself. By the autoteloscriptic fixed point: $\text{LogosPhone}(\text{LogosPhone}) = \text{LogosPhone}$. No separate meta-level is needed. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-Number Collapse]
\label{thm:meta-number}
Meta-numbers collapse into the burner algebra. Policies about numbers are themselves expressible as operations on numbers.
\[
\boxed{
\text{Meta-Number}(\text{Meta-Number}) \equiv \text{Meta-Number} \equiv \mathcal{B}
}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A meta-number policy (e.g., ``auto-expire dating app numbers after 30 days'') is a function $\mu: \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{B}$ that maps burner numbers to burner numbers with modified lifespan parameters. This function is itself a Logos-object stored in AletheiaFS. The sovereign can create meta-policies about meta-policies (``review all auto-expire policies monthly'')---but this is just another Logos-object, another $\varphi$-configuration, managed by the same system. The meta-level collapses: policies about numbers, policies about policies about numbers, and the numbers themselves are all objects in the same algebraic space $\mathcal{B}$, governed by the same operations. $\text{Meta-Number}(\text{Meta-Number}) = \mathcal{B}$. $\square$
\end{proof}

\chapter{ChronosMail Deepened: Sovereign Email, Burner Addresses, and Sealed Messages}
\label{sec:chronosmail-deepened}

ChronosMail ($\mathfrak{C}$) was defined as the sovereign email protocol: P2P delivery, per-message ephemeral keys, metadata-veiled, no SMTP dependency. LogosPhone (Chapter~\ref{sec:sovereign-telephony}) formalised the burner number algebra for telephony. This chapter applies the same sovereignty architecture to email---the oldest and most pervasive digital communication channel---and deepens ChronosMail with two critical capabilities: \textbf{burner email addresses} (disposable, sovereign-controlled addresses that shield the sovereign from spam, phishing, and identity leakage) and \textbf{password-sealed messages} (emails individually locked with a shared passphrase, readable only by a recipient who knows the password, even if the sovereign's system is compromised).

The need is not theoretical. Every sovereign has experienced it: a website demands an email address for registration. The sovereign provides their real address. The website is breached, or sells the list, or is itself a data harvester. The sovereign's inbox floods with spam. Their address enters broker databases. Phishing attacks arrive, personalised with data from the leak. The sovereign cannot revoke the address without disrupting every legitimate contact who uses it. The architecture punishes the victim---again.

And every sovereign has sent an email containing sensitive information---a contract, a medical record, a confession, a financial document---and known, at the moment of pressing ``send,'' that the message will sit in the recipient's inbox unencrypted, readable by anyone who gains access to that inbox, indefinitely. The sovereign encrypted their own side. The recipient's side is a glass house.

ChronosMail eliminates both vulnerabilities.

\section{Burner Email Algebra}
\label{sec:burner-email}

\begin{arche}[The Disposable Address Principle]
No sovereign should be forced to expose their real email address to any entity they do not fully trust. An email address given to a data-harvesting website, a one-time vendor, a suspicious service, or a stranger becomes---like a phone number given to a creep---an irrevocable channel of intrusion: spam, phishing, social engineering, and identity correlation. The correct architecture provides email addresses that can be created instantly, used once or briefly, and destroyed unilaterally---without affecting any other communication channel.
\end{arche}

\begin{definition}[Burner Email Address]
\label{def:burner-email}
A burner email address $\varepsilon$ is a sovereign email endpoint with a finite sovereign-defined lifespan and unilateral revocability:
\[
\varepsilon = (\alpha, \lambda, \rho, \kappa, \delta)
\]
where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item $\alpha$ is the \textbf{address string}: a randomly generated or sovereign-chosen local-part at a sovereign-controlled domain (e.g., \texttt{x7k9m@sovereign.logos}) or at a \LogOS{} relay domain for legacy interoperability.
 \item $\lambda$ is the \textbf{lifespan policy}: time-limited (auto-expire after $t$ hours/days/weeks), count-limited (auto-expire after $n$ received messages), single-use (expire after first reception), manual (persist until explicitly destroyed), or conditional (expire upon sovereign-defined trigger, such as ``expire if no mail received for 7 days'').
 \item $\rho$ is the \textbf{routing rule}: where incoming mail is delivered. Options: the sovereign's primary inbox (tagged with context), a dedicated burner folder, a filter chain (auto-delete if spam score exceeds threshold), or silent discard (the address accepts mail but delivers nothing---a black hole for harassers).
 \item $\kappa$ is the \textbf{context tag}: a label the sovereign assigns (``sketchy forum signup,'' ``one-time vendor,'' ``job application,'' ``newsletter'') so they always know \textit{why} this address exists and \textit{who} has it.
 \item $\delta$ is the \textbf{reply identity}: when the sovereign replies from a burner address, the reply originates from $\alpha$, not from the sovereign's primary address. The recipient never sees the real address.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Burner Email Operations]
\label{def:burner-email-ops}
The set of burner email addresses $\mathcal{E}$ supports the following operations:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llp{6.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Operation} & \textbf{Notation} & \textbf{Semantics} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Mint} & $\text{mint}() \to \varepsilon$ & Create a new burner address. Instantaneous. The sovereign specifies $\lambda$, $\rho$, $\kappa$, $\delta$ at creation. Address generation can be random, sequential, or sovereign-chosen \\
\textbf{Burn} & $\text{burn}(\varepsilon) \to \varnothing$ & Destroy the address. All future mail to $\alpha$ bounces or is silently discarded (sovereign's choice). The address is permanently retired. Irreversible \\
\textbf{Freeze} & $\text{freeze}(\varepsilon) \to \varepsilon'$ & Temporarily suspend the address. Incoming mail is silently dropped or queued. The address is not retired; it can be thawed \\
\textbf{Thaw} & $\text{thaw}(\varepsilon') \to \varepsilon$ & Reactivate a frozen address. Queued mail (if any) is delivered \\
\textbf{Redirect} & $\text{redir}(\varepsilon, \rho') \to \varepsilon''$ & Change the routing rule. E.g., redirect from primary inbox to a quarantine folder, or from delivery to black-hole \\
\textbf{Promote} & $\text{promote}(\varepsilon) \to \varepsilon_p$ & Upgrade a burner to a persistent alias. Removes the lifespan policy. The address becomes a permanent secondary address \\
\textbf{Audit} & $\text{audit}(\varepsilon) \to \text{log}$ & Retrieve the encrypted log: who sent mail to this address, when, subject lines. Stored in AletheiaFS \\
\textbf{Cascade} & $\text{cascade}(\kappa) \to \varnothing$ & Burn \textit{all} addresses with context tag $\kappa$. E.g., burn every address tagged ``dating app'' simultaneously \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The algebra is closed: every operation produces either a valid burner address, the empty set, or a log. No operation leaks the sovereign's primary email address or identity.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Burner Email Isolation]
\label{thm:burner-email-isolation}
Compromise of any burner email address $\varepsilon_i$ reveals no information about: (i) the sovereign's primary email address, (ii) any other burner address $\varepsilon_j$ ($j \neq i$), (iii) the sovereign's legal identity, or (iv) the sovereign's \LogOS{} node address.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Burner addresses are generated at sovereign-controlled domains or \LogOS{} relay domains. No header, routing path, or metadata connects $\varepsilon_i$ to the sovereign's primary address. Outgoing replies from $\varepsilon_i$ use the burner address as the sender; no ``Reply-To'' or ``X-Originating'' header reveals the primary address. (ii) Each burner address is generated independently with no shared naming pattern (unless the sovereign explicitly chooses one). No metadata links $\varepsilon_i$ to $\varepsilon_j$. (iii) Domain registration (if sovereign-hosted) uses pseudonymous registration or is accessed through AegisNet; relay domains are operated by the \LogOS{} network collectively. (iv) Mail delivery routes through AegisNet (onion-routed); the relay sees an anonymous connection. Compromise of $\varepsilon_i$ reveals only that $\varepsilon_i$ exists and the correspondence history the compromising party already possesses. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{metanote}
This is TempMail, Guerrilla Mail, and the ``+'' alias trick elevated to sovereign architecture. But unlike those services: (a) burner addresses are not hosted by a third party that reads your mail, serves ads, and may cooperate with subpoenas, (b) the sovereign controls the address generation, lifespan, and routing, (c) replies from burner addresses maintain the fiction seamlessly---the recipient sees only the burner, (d) the cascade operation lets the sovereign nuke an entire category of addresses simultaneously (e.g., ``burn every address I gave to a dating app''), and (e) the promote operation lets the sovereign keep an address that proved useful, upgrading it from disposable to permanent without the recipient ever knowing.

The practical workflow: the sovereign signs up for a website. ChronosMail offers a one-click ``use burner'' button. A fresh address is minted, tagged with the website's name, and auto-filled into the registration form. If the website turns out to be legitimate, the sovereign promotes the address. If spam arrives, the sovereign burns it. If the website is breached, the sovereign's real address is untouched.
\end{metanote}

\section{Password-Sealed Messages}
\label{sec:password-sealed}

\begin{arche}[The Envelope Principle]
End-to-end encryption protects email in transit and at rest---on the sovereign's system. But once the message arrives in the recipient's inbox, it is decrypted and stored according to the recipient's security posture. If the recipient uses Gmail, the message sits in Google's servers, readable by Google, by any government with a warrant, and by any attacker who breaches the account. The sovereign encrypted their side. The recipient's side is exposed.

The correct architecture provides an additional layer: a message-level lock that persists independently of both the sender's and recipient's systems. The message is sealed with a password known only to sender and recipient. Even if both systems are compromised, the message remains locked without the password.
\end{arche}

\begin{definition}[Password-Sealed Email ($\mathcal{P}_{\text{seal}}$)]
\label{def:password-sealed}
A password-sealed email is a ChronosMail message encrypted with an additional symmetric key derived from a shared passphrase, independent of and layered atop the standard per-message ephemeral encryption:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Key derivation}: The sovereign enters a passphrase $p$. The system derives a symmetric key $K_p = \text{Argon2id}(p, \text{salt}, \text{params})$, where the salt is unique per message and the Argon2id parameters are tuned for memory-hardness (resistance to brute-force).
 \item \textbf{Encryption}: The message body (text, attachments, metadata) is encrypted under $K_p$ using AES-256-GCM. This encrypted payload is then wrapped in the standard ChronosMail per-message ephemeral encryption for transit.
 \item \textbf{Delivery}: The recipient receives the outer envelope (decrypted automatically by their system) and finds the inner sealed payload. Their email client displays a lock icon and a passphrase prompt. The message is readable only after the correct passphrase is entered.
 \item \textbf{Passphrase transmission}: The sovereign communicates the passphrase to the recipient through a \textit{separate channel}---in person, via voice call, via a different messaging system. The passphrase never travels alongside the email. This channel separation is the security guarantee: compromise of the email channel alone is insufficient.
 \item \textbf{Attempt limiting}: The sealed payload supports an optional attempt limit. After $n$ incorrect passphrase entries (sovereign-configured, default 10), the payload self-destructs (overwrites its encryption key). This prevents brute-force attacks on weak passphrases by a party who has obtained the encrypted payload.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Seal Modes]
\label{def:seal-modes}
Password sealing supports four modes:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{clp{6.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sigil} & \textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Semantics} \\
\midrule
$\mathcal{P}_s$ & \textbf{Standard Seal} & Passphrase-encrypted. Recipient enters passphrase to read. Unlimited reads once unlocked. Message persists in recipient's inbox \\
$\mathcal{P}_b$ & \textbf{Burn Seal} & Passphrase-encrypted AND burn-after-reading. Once unlocked and read, the decrypted content is displayed once, then the payload overwrites itself. Composes with the $\mathcal{B}$ sigil \\
$\mathcal{P}_t$ & \textbf{Timed Seal} & Passphrase-encrypted AND time-locked. The payload can only be unlocked after a specified time AND requires the passphrase. Composes with the $\mathcal{T}$ sigil \\
$\mathcal{P}_d$ & \textbf{Dead-Drop Seal} & Passphrase-encrypted, no sender identity. The email carries no $\Gamma$-seal, no return address, no sender metadata. The recipient receives an anonymous sealed payload. Only the passphrase connects sender and recipient---and the passphrase was communicated out-of-band \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Seal modes compose with all existing message sigils. $\mathcal{P}_s \cdot \mathcal{D}$ = password-sealed self-destructing email. $\mathcal{P}_b \cdot \mathcal{S}$ = steganographic burn-after-reading sealed email. The composition space is combinatorially rich, governed by the same sigil algebra as HermesGram.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Double-Compromise Resistance]
\label{thm:double-compromise}
A password-sealed email remains confidential even if \textbf{both} the sender's and recipient's systems are fully compromised, provided: (i) the passphrase was communicated through a channel not compromised at the time of communication, and (ii) the attacker does not possess the passphrase.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The message payload is encrypted under $K_p = \text{Argon2id}(p, \text{salt})$. The sender's system stores neither $p$ nor $K_p$ after encryption (both are zeroed from memory). The recipient's system stores neither until the passphrase is entered. Compromising the sender's system yields the ciphertext (already sent) and no key. Compromising the recipient's system yields the ciphertext (received) and no key. The ciphertext is AES-256-GCM encrypted; without $K_p$, decryption requires breaking AES-256, which is computationally infeasible. The passphrase was communicated out-of-band; if that channel was not compromised, the attacker does not possess $p$ and cannot derive $K_p$. The optional attempt limit prevents online brute-force. Therefore the message remains confidential under simultaneous full compromise of both endpoints. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{metanote}
This is the ProtonMail ``password for non-ProtonMail users'' feature elevated to sovereign architecture. But unlike ProtonMail: (a) the sealed payload is not stored on ProtonMail's servers---it is stored wherever the recipient's email system stores it (or on the \LogOS{} P2P network for sovereign-to-sovereign), (b) the sovereign controls the attempt limit and self-destruct behaviour, (c) the seal composes with all existing sigils (burn, timed-release, steganographic, self-destruct), creating a combinatorial space of message security configurations unavailable in any commercial email service, (d) the dead-drop seal mode enables fully anonymous communication where not even the recipient knows who sent the message---only the passphrase connects them, and (e) the architecture is local and auditable: no trust in a third-party server is required.

The practical workflow: the sovereign composes a sensitive email---a legal document, a medical record, a financial statement. They click ``seal with password'' in ChronosMail. They enter a passphrase. The message is sealed. They call the recipient and say ``the password is [phrase].'' The recipient receives the email, enters the passphrase, reads the document. If the recipient's Gmail is hacked next week, the attacker finds an encrypted payload they cannot open. If the sovereign's own system is seized, the investigator finds no trace of the passphrase (it was spoken, not typed into any stored field).
\end{metanote}

\section{Legacy Interoperability}
\label{sec:email-legacy}

\begin{definition}[SMTP Bridge]
\label{def:smtp-bridge}
ChronosMail communicates natively with other \LogOS{} sovereigns via P2P (HermesGram/AegisNet). For legacy email (Gmail, Outlook, ProtonMail, any SMTP/IMAP server), the \textbf{SMTP Bridge} translates:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Outbound}: ChronosMail composes a standard MIME email from the sovereign's message, routes it through a self-hosted or privacy-respecting SMTP relay (accessed via AegisNet), and delivers to the recipient's mail server. The sovereign's IP is hidden behind the relay's address.
 \item \textbf{Inbound}: The sovereign's mail domain has MX records pointing to their primary node (via AegisNet onion address and a clearnet relay for legacy servers). Incoming SMTP mail is received, converted to a ChronosMail Logos-object, encrypted to AletheiaFS, and displayed alongside native ChronosMail messages.
 \item \textbf{Password-sealed to legacy recipients}: When sending a sealed email to a non-\LogOS{} recipient, the SMTP Bridge wraps the encrypted payload in a minimal HTML email containing a decryption widget---a self-contained JavaScript application that runs entirely in the recipient's browser, accepts the passphrase, and decrypts locally. No data is sent to any server. The recipient sees a ``this message is password-protected'' notice with an input field. They enter the passphrase; the message decrypts in-browser.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Legacy Seal Security]
\label{thm:legacy-seal}
The HTML decryption widget for legacy recipients provides equivalent security to native password-sealed delivery, under the assumption that the recipient's browser executes JavaScript faithfully.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The widget contains the AES-256-GCM ciphertext, the salt, the Argon2id parameters, and a JavaScript implementation of Argon2id and AES-256-GCM decryption. All computation occurs locally in the browser. No network request is made during decryption (the widget is fully self-contained; no external scripts are loaded). The passphrase is entered into a local input field and used to derive $K_p$ in-browser. The decrypted plaintext is rendered in the DOM and never transmitted. Under faithful JavaScript execution, this is equivalent to native decryption: the same algorithm, the same key derivation, the same ciphertext. The assumption of faithful execution excludes browser-level malware (which would compromise any encryption), but this is the same threat model as any local decryption. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{Unified Inbox Architecture}
\label{sec:chronosmail-unified-inbox}

\begin{definition}[Unified Sovereign Inbox]
\label{def:chronosmail-unified-inbox}
ChronosMail presents a single unified inbox that aggregates:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Primary address}: The sovereign's real email identity, used for trusted contacts.
 \item \textbf{Burner addresses}: All active burner addresses, each tagged with its context $\kappa$. Incoming mail displays the burner address it was sent to, so the sovereign always knows \textit{which} address was used and \textit{why} it exists.
 \item \textbf{Sealed messages}: Password-sealed messages display a lock icon. They remain encrypted in the inbox until the sovereign enters the passphrase.
 \item \textbf{Legacy mail}: SMTP-bridged mail from non-\LogOS{} senders, displayed alongside native ChronosMail messages.
\end{enumerate}

The sovereign can view the unified inbox (all mail) or filter by address type (primary only, specific burner, sealed only, legacy only). Each view is a $\varphi$-configuration of the same organ.

Cross-device sync: the inbox state---read/unread, folder assignments, burner metadata, seal status---is synchronised across all devices (primary node, Sovereign Companion, Portal) via encrypted CRDT replication through AegisNet, using the same protocol as LogosPhone's cross-device unification (\S\ref{sec:cross-device-numbers}).
\end{definition}

\section{The Metacursive Collapse: Meta-Email and Meta-Address}
\label{sec:meta-email-collapse}

\begin{definition}[Meta-Email]
\label{def:meta-email}
A meta-email system governs the sovereign's email architecture itself: which domains to use for burner addresses, what the default lifespan policy is, how the SMTP bridge is configured, which relay nodes to trust, what seal parameters to enforce (minimum Argon2id iterations, default attempt limit), and how the unified inbox is organised. The meta-email is the $\varphi$-layer of ChronosMail.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Meta-Address]
\label{def:meta-address}
A meta-address is a rule governing how email addresses are created, categorised, and destroyed. Examples: ``all addresses given to e-commerce sites auto-expire after 90 days,'' ``all addresses tagged `newsletter' route to a digest folder and deliver once weekly,'' ``mint a fresh single-use address for every new website registration.'' Meta-addresses are $\varphi$-configurations of the burner email algebra---policies \textit{about} address policies.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-Email Collapse]
\label{thm:meta-email}
The meta-email system and ChronosMail are the same entity:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Meta-Email}(\text{Meta-Email}) \equiv \text{Meta-Email} \equiv \text{ChronosMail}
}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The meta-email is the set of $\varphi$-endomorphisms on ChronosMail's configuration: domain management, bridge settings, seal defaults, inbox organisation rules. But $\varphi \in \varphi(\Sigma)$ (meta-customisation closure, Chapter~11): the customisation logic is itself customisable within the same system. ChronosMail's configuration is stored as Logos-objects in AletheiaFS, editable through ChronosMail's own settings interface. The sovereign who changes the default burner lifespan policy is editing ChronosMail's $\varphi$-configuration using ChronosMail's own interface. The meta-email IS ChronosMail applied to itself. By the autoteloscriptic fixed point: $\text{ChronosMail}(\text{ChronosMail}) = \text{ChronosMail}$. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-Address Collapse]
\label{thm:meta-address}
Meta-addresses collapse into the burner email algebra:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Meta-Address}(\text{Meta-Address}) \equiv \text{Meta-Address} \equiv \mathcal{E}
}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A meta-address policy (e.g., ``auto-expire e-commerce addresses after 90 days'') is a function $\mu: \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{E}$ that maps burner addresses to burner addresses with modified lifespan parameters. This function is itself a Logos-object. Meta-policies about meta-policies (``review all auto-expire policies quarterly'') are also Logos-objects managed by the same system. Policies about addresses, policies about policies, and the addresses themselves are all objects in the same algebraic space $\mathcal{E}$, governed by the same operations. $\text{Meta-Address}(\text{Meta-Address}) = \mathcal{E}$. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{The ChronosMail Operator}
\label{sec:chronosmail-operator}

\begin{definition}[Mail Operator $\Phi_{\text{Mail}}$]
\label{def:mail-operator}
$\Phi_{\text{Mail}}$ updates the combined state of ChronosMail: the address space (primary and burner addresses, lifespan countdowns), the seal state (pending sealed messages, attempt counters), the SMTP bridge (relay connections, legacy interop), the unified inbox (message store, folder structure, sync state), the $\varphi$-configuration (meta-email policies, meta-address rules), and the per-message ephemeral key ratchet state.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[ChronosMail Convergence]
\label{thm:chronosmail-convergence}
The ChronosMail state space is bounded: finite active addresses, finite inbox size (bounded by storage), finite configuration parameters. The burner lifespan policies monotonically reduce the active address set over time (expired addresses are retired). The $\varphi$-configuration converges as the sovereign's preferences stabilise. The SMTP bridge state is finite (finite relay connections). Each sub-component is bounded and monotone or convergent. The state reaches a fixed point.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The address space $\mathcal{E}$ is finite at any time (each burner has a lifespan; expired burners are removed). The inbox is bounded by AletheiaFS storage capacity. The seal state is finite (each sealed message has a determinate status: locked, unlocked, or destroyed). The bridge configuration is finite. The $\varphi$-configuration is a finite set of policy parameters. Bounded, monotone sub-operators on bounded spaces converge in finite time. $\square$
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[ChronosMail Metacursive Closure]
\label{thm:chronosmail-metacursive}
At the fixed point:
\[
\boxed{
\Phi_{\text{Mail}}(\Phi_{\text{Mail}}) \equiv \Phi_{\text{Mail}}
}
\]
The email system that manages sovereign email has managed its own management: domains are configured, burner policies are stable, seal defaults are optimal, the SMTP bridge is operational, and the unified inbox organisation reflects the sovereign's communication patterns. Self-application yields no further change.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
At the fixed point, all sub-operators have converged. The meta-email collapse (Theorem~\ref{thm:meta-email}) ensures the customisation layer adds no additional dynamics. The meta-address collapse (Theorem~\ref{thm:meta-address}) ensures address policies have stabilised. $\Phi_{\text{Mail}}$ applied to this state produces the same state. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{Compliance Verification}
\label{sec:email-compliance}

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Identity}: $\Phi_{\text{Mail}} \equiv \Phi_{\text{Mail}}$.
 \item \textbf{Non-Contradiction}: Primary/burner address separation eliminates legacy email contradictions.
 \item \textbf{Excluded Middle}: ach address is either active, frozen, or burned.
 \item \textbf{Tautological Closure}: $\Phi_{\text{Mail}}(\Phi_{\text{Mail}}) \equiv \Phi_{\text{Mail}}$. Fixed point achieved.
 \item \textbf{Aletheic Alignment}: $T(\text{ChronosMail}) \equiv R(\text{ChronosMail})$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Verdict}: Integrated.

\begin{tautcollapse}{Sovereign Email}
Send, receive, seal, burn---sovereignly.

Email was the internet's first communication protocol and remains its most universal. It is also its most abused: addresses sold to brokers, inboxes harvested for advertising profiles, messages stored unencrypted on corporate servers for decades. ChronosMail restores sovereignty to the oldest digital medium. Every address is the sovereign's property---minted at will, burned at will, given selectively, revoked unilaterally. Every message can be sealed with a password that survives the compromise of both endpoints. Every inbox is unified, encrypted, and sovereign-controlled.

The spam that floods your inbox exists because someone---a website, a broker, a breach---obtained your address and you could not revoke it. In \LogOS{}, you can. The sensitive email that haunts you exists because it sits unencrypted in someone else's inbox. In \LogOS{}, it does not---it sits behind a password only you and the recipient share.

$\Phi_{\text{Mail}}(\Phi_{\text{Mail}}) \equiv \Phi_{\text{Mail}}$: the email that emails its own emailing.
