\chapter{Applied Quantum Sovereignty: Engineering the Meta-Quantum Architecture}
\label{sec:applied-quantum}

The Meta-Quantum Ontology (Ch.~\ref{sec:meta-quantum}) established the theoretical ground: wave collapse as self-recognition, encryption as controlled potentiality, computation as the interplay between superposition and determination. This chapter translates that ontology into \textbf{concrete engineering}: what quantum technologies exist today, what is arriving within the decade, and how \LogOS{} integrates each into its sovereign architecture---from Nigredo (using available quantum resources through classical interfaces) through Rubedo (sovereign quantum hardware under the sovereign's direct control).

The critical insight: quantum technologies are not science fiction. Quantum random number generators are commercially available for under \$100. Post-quantum cryptographic algorithms are standardised (NIST FIPS 203, 204, 205---August 2024). Quantum key distribution networks operate in several countries. Small quantum processors are accessible via cloud APIs. \LogOS{} integrates all of these---not as future speculation but as \textbf{present-day engineering choices} that deepen the sovereign's security, privacy, and computational power.

\section{Quantum Random Number Generation (QRNG)}
\label{sec:qrng}

\begin{definition}[The Randomness Problem]
\label{def:randomness-problem}
Every cryptographic system depends on randomness: key generation, nonces, initialisation vectors, padding, session identifiers, and challenge values all require unpredictable random numbers. Classical computers generate \textbf{pseudo-random} numbers (PRNGs): deterministic algorithms that produce sequences that \textit{appear} random but are entirely determined by an initial seed. If an adversary learns the seed, every ``random'' number is predictable. Even hardware random number generators (HRNGs) in conventional CPUs (Intel's RDRAND, AMD's RRNG) rely on physical noise sources (thermal noise, jitter) that are \textit{believed} to be unpredictable but are not \textit{provably} so---an adversary with sufficient physical access or side-channel capability might bias or predict the output.

True randomness---randomness that is provably unpredictable even to an adversary with unlimited computational power---requires a \textbf{fundamentally non-deterministic} process. Quantum mechanics provides exactly this: the outcome of a quantum measurement is inherently random. Not pseudo-random. Not ``random as far as we can tell.'' \textit{Provably, fundamentally, irreducibly random}---guaranteed by the laws of physics (specifically, the Born rule: $P(|s_i\rangle) = |\alpha_i|^2$, with no underlying deterministic mechanism).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sovereign QRNG Integration ($\mathcal{R}_Q$)]
\label{def:qrng-integration}
\LogOS{} integrates quantum random number generation at the kernel level:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Nigredo (Available Now)}: USB-attached QRNG devices (e.g., Quantis by ID Quantique, ComScire PQ series, or open-hardware designs based on photon detection) connect to the sovereign's machine. LogosKernel exposes the QRNG via \texttt{/dev/qrandom}---a character device providing true quantum random bytes. The kernel's entropy pool (which normally mixes HRNG output, interrupt timing, and user input) is \textbf{seeded} by the QRNG. All cryptographic operations draw from this quantum-seeded pool.

 Cost: USB QRNG devices range from \$50--\$500. Output: 4--16 Mbit/s of true random data. This exceeds the entropy consumption of even heavy cryptographic workloads by orders of magnitude.

 \item \textbf{Albedo (Near-Term)}: Cloud QRNG services (provided by quantum hardware vendors) deliver quantum random numbers via API. \LogOS{} treats these as a \textit{supplementary} source---never as the sole source (the cloud provider could tamper with the output). The kernel mixes cloud QRNG output with local QRNG and HRNG sources. No single source is trusted exclusively.

 \item \textbf{Rubedo (Target)}: The sovereign quantum module (see \S\ref{sec:sovereign-quantum-hw}) includes an integrated QRNG---a photonic chip generating quantum random numbers at Gbit/s rates directly on the sovereign's hardware. No USB device. No cloud service. No external trust. The randomness is generated by physics inside the sovereign's machine, under the sovereign's physical control.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Kernel Integration}: The QRNG feeds into the Autoclave's (\S\ref{sec:meta-cryptoanalysis}) key generation pipeline. PrimeKey derivation, session key generation, nonce selection, and all cryptographic initialisation vectors use QRNG output when available. When no QRNG is present, the system falls back to the Linux kernel's \texttt{/dev/urandom} (which is cryptographically secure but not provably random). The sovereign is informed of their randomness source via $\Omega$-Vigilance: ``Entropy source: QRNG (hardware)'' vs.\ ``Entropy source: HRNG (software).''
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[QRNG Security Advantage]
\label{thm:qrng-advantage}
A system using QRNG for key generation is immune to entropy-depletion attacks, PRNG state-recovery attacks, and seed-prediction attacks. These attack classes are eliminated (not merely made harder) because the random numbers have no seed, no state, and no deterministic algorithm to reverse.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Entropy depletion: A PRNG can ``run out of entropy'' if the entropy pool is not replenished, producing predictable output. A QRNG generates fresh entropy from quantum measurements continuously---it cannot deplete because each measurement is an independent quantum event. (ii) State recovery: A PRNG has internal state; recovering the state (via memory dump, side-channel, or cold-boot attack) reveals all future output. A QRNG has no exploitable state---the next output is determined by a future quantum event that has not yet occurred. (iii) Seed prediction: A PRNG is determined by its seed. A QRNG has no seed. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{Post-Quantum Cryptographic Architecture}
\label{sec:pqc-architecture}

\begin{definition}[The Quantum Threat Model]
\label{def:quantum-threat}
A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can factor large integers and compute discrete logarithms in polynomial time, breaking:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{RSA}: Security rests on integer factorisation. Broken by Shor's.
 \item \textbf{Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)}: Security rests on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. Broken by Shor's. This includes ECDH, ECDSA, Ed25519, X25519.
 \item \textbf{Diffie-Hellman}: Security rests on the discrete logarithm problem. Broken by Shor's.
\end{enumerate}
Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for brute-force search, effectively halving the security level of symmetric ciphers (AES-256 becomes AES-128 equivalent). This is addressed by doubling key sizes.

The ``Harvest Now, Decrypt Later'' (HNDL) threat is present \textit{today}: nation-state adversaries collect encrypted communications now, intending to decrypt them when quantum computers become available. Data encrypted today with RSA or ECC may be readable within 10--15 years. For sovereign data with long-term sensitivity (identity keys, financial records, personal history), this threat is immediate.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[LogOS Post-Quantum Cryptographic Stack]
\label{def:pqc-stack}
\LogOS{}'s cryptographic stack (specified in Ch.~14, Autotelocrypta) is already post-quantum by default. The complete specification:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lp{3cm}p{3cm}p{3.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Function} & \textbf{Algorithm} & \textbf{Standard} & \textbf{Security Basis} \\
\midrule
Key Encapsulation & \textbf{ML-KEM-1024} (Kyber) & NIST FIPS 203 & Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) lattice problem \\
Digital Signature & \textbf{ML-DSA-65} (Dilithium) & NIST FIPS 204 & MLWE + SelfTargetMSIS lattice problem \\
Hash-Based Signature & \textbf{SLH-DSA} (SPHINCS+) & NIST FIPS 205 & Hash function security only (most conservative) \\
Symmetric Encryption & \textbf{ChaCha20-Poly1305} & IETF RFC 8439 & 256-bit symmetric (128-bit post-quantum via Grover) \\
Hashing & \textbf{BLAKE3} & (de facto standard) & 256-bit hash (128-bit post-quantum) \\
Key Derivation & \textbf{Argon2id} & IETF RFC 9106 & Memory-hard; resistant to ASIC/GPU/quantum \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Crypto-Agility ($\mathcal{A}_C$)]
\label{def:crypto-agility}
Post-quantum cryptography is an active research field. Algorithms believed secure today may be broken tomorrow (SIKE, a NIST PQC finalist, was completely broken in 2022 by a classical attack). \LogOS{} therefore implements \textbf{crypto-agility}: the ability to replace any cryptographic algorithm without rewriting the system:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Algorithm abstraction layer}: Every cryptographic operation in \LogOS{} is performed through an abstract interface (KEM, Signature, AEAD, Hash, KDF). The concrete algorithm is selected by the $\varphi$-configuration. Changing $\varphi$ changes the algorithm without changing any calling code.
 \item \textbf{Hybrid mode (default)}: All key exchanges use \textbf{both} a classical algorithm (X25519) and a post-quantum algorithm (ML-KEM-1024) simultaneously. The shared secret is the concatenation of both key exchanges, hashed together. Security: if \textit{either} algorithm is secure, the combined key is secure. The classical algorithm protects against the possibility that the PQ algorithm is broken by a classical attack (like SIKE). The PQ algorithm protects against quantum computers. Both must be broken for the hybrid to fail.
 \item \textbf{Hot-swap protocol}: When a cryptographic algorithm is deprecated (via Advisory Update), the system:
 \begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*., noitemsep]
 \item Generates new keys under the replacement algorithm.
 \item Re-encrypts stored data incrementally (background process, prioritised by sensitivity).
 \item Notifies peers of the new public keys via LogosIPC/AegisNet.
 \item Revokes old keys after a grace period.
 \end{enumerate}
 The hot-swap is atomic per-session: no session uses a mix of old and new algorithms. All operations during transition use the stronger of the two available algorithms.
 \item \textbf{Algorithm governance}: The sovereign retains ultimate authority over which algorithms are used. Advisory Updates \textit{recommend} algorithm changes. The sovereign can accept, defer, or reject. No algorithm is forced. The system explains the risk: ``ML-KEM-1024 is recommended because [reason]. Your current algorithm [X] has [status]. Accept migration?''
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Crypto-Agility Convergence]
\label{thm:crypto-agility}
The crypto-agility system converges to the strongest available configuration. Let $A_t$ denote the set of available algorithms at time $t$ and $S(a)$ the security level of algorithm $a$. The $\varphi$-configuration selects $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in A_t} S(a)$ subject to the sovereign's constraints (device capability, performance requirements, sovereign override). When a new algorithm $a'$ enters $A_t$ with $S(a') > S(a^*)$, the Advisory Update recommends migration. When an algorithm $a''$ is broken ($S(a'') \to 0$), the hot-swap removes it. The system monotonically increases in security strength over time, bounded only by the state of the art.
\end{theorem}

\section{Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)}
\label{sec:qkd}

\begin{definition}[Quantum Key Distribution]
\label{def:qkd}
QKD uses quantum mechanics to distribute encryption keys with \textbf{information-theoretic security}: security guaranteed by the laws of physics, not by computational hardness. An eavesdropper cannot intercept the key without disturbing the quantum states, revealing their presence.

The BB84 protocol (Bennett \& Brassard, 1984):
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item Alice generates random bits and encodes each in a random basis (rectilinear $+$ or diagonal $\times$) as the polarisation of a single photon.
 \item Alice sends the photons to Bob over a quantum channel (optical fibre or free-space laser).
 \item Bob measures each photon in a randomly chosen basis.
 \item Alice and Bob publicly compare bases (not results). They keep only the bits where they chose the same basis ($\sim$50\% of bits).
 \item They sacrifice a subset of matching bits to check for eavesdropping: if an eavesdropper (Eve) measured the photons, the error rate exceeds the quantum bit error rate threshold (typically $\sim$11\%). If the error rate is below threshold, the remaining bits form a shared secret key.
 \item Privacy amplification: the raw key is hashed to eliminate any information Eve may have gained. The result is a provably secure shared key.
\end{enumerate}

Security guarantee: the no-cloning theorem (a quantum state cannot be perfectly copied) means Eve cannot intercept and forward the photons without introducing detectable errors. This is not a computational assumption---it is a physical law.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[LogOS QKD Integration]
\label{def:qkd-integration}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Nigredo (Available Now in Limited Contexts)}: QKD networks operate in China (Beijing--Shanghai, 2,000+ km), Europe (EuroQCI initiative), South Korea, Japan, and select US metropolitan areas. These networks provide QKD-secured links between \textit{fixed endpoints} connected by optical fibre. A sovereign connected to a QKD network (via a QKD terminal device, typically a rack-mounted photonic unit) can establish QKD-secured channels with other QKD-connected sovereigns.

 LogOS integration: AegisNet detects QKD-capable links and transparently uses QKD-distributed keys for those connections. The key management is handled by the Autoclave, which stores QKD keys in the same PrimeKey hierarchy as all other keys. To the sovereign, the experience is identical---messages are encrypted as always. The difference is invisible but profound: the keys are provably secure, not merely computationally secure.

 Limitation: QKD currently requires dedicated optical fibre between endpoints. It does not work over the internet. Range is limited ($\sim$100 km per fibre span without quantum repeaters). This restricts QKD to sovereign-to-sovereign links in metropolitan areas or between institutions connected by dark fibre.

 \item \textbf{Albedo (Near-Term, 3--10 Years)}: Satellite QKD (demonstrated by China's Micius satellite, 2017) extends QKD to global distances. Low-earth-orbit satellites distribute entangled photons to ground stations, enabling key exchange between any two ground stations with line-of-sight to the satellite. The EU's IRIS\textsuperscript{2} constellation and China's QSS programme are deploying satellite QKD.

 LogOS integration: Sovereign ground station hardware (a telescope and single-photon detector, potentially commodity hardware at scale) connects to QKD satellites. AegisNet routes key exchange through satellite QKD when available, falling back to post-quantum classical crypto otherwise. The routing decision is automatic: AegisNet selects the strongest available channel.

 \item \textbf{Rubedo (Target)}: Quantum repeaters and quantum memories enable \textit{quantum internet}: end-to-end quantum channels between arbitrary endpoints, mediated by a network of repeater nodes that extend entanglement over arbitrary distances. At Rubedo, every sovereign node is a quantum network endpoint. Key exchange between any two sovereigns uses entanglement distribution (E91 protocol or successors), providing information-theoretic security globally.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[QKD Security Composition]
\label{thm:qkd-composition}
\LogOS{}'s hybrid security model composes QKD with post-quantum classical crypto:
\[
K_{\text{session}} = \text{BLAKE3}(K_{\text{QKD}} \| K_{\text{ML-KEM}} \| K_{\text{X25519}})
\]
The session key is derived from the concatenation of (i) the QKD key (information-theoretically secure), (ii) the post-quantum KEM key (computationally secure against quantum), and (iii) the classical ECDH key (computationally secure against classical). If \textbf{any one} of the three is secure, the session key is secure. This is defence in depth across three independent security foundations: physics (QKD), lattice hardness (ML-KEM), and ECDLP hardness (X25519).
\end{theorem}

\section{Quantum Computing as Sovereign Resource}
\label{sec:quantum-computing-resource}

\begin{definition}[The Quantum Computing Landscape (2024--2030)]
\label{def:qc-landscape}
Quantum computers are real but limited. The current state:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ)} devices: 50--1,000+ qubits, high error rates ($10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$ per gate), limited coherence times. Available via cloud: IBM Quantum, Google Quantum AI, Amazon Braket, Azure Quantum, IonQ, Rigetti.
 \item \textbf{Error-corrected quantum computers}: Not yet available. Require $\sim$1,000--10,000 physical qubits per logical qubit. Estimated timeline: 2028--2035 for useful error-corrected computation.
 \item \textbf{Quantum annealers}: D-Wave systems (5,000+ qubits) for optimisation problems. Available now via cloud. Not universal quantum computers but useful for specific problem classes.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[LogOS Quantum Compute Integration ($\mathcal{Q}_C$)]
\label{def:quantum-compute}
\LogOS{} treats quantum computing as a \textbf{heterogeneous compute resource}---analogous to how modern systems use GPUs for parallel computation alongside CPUs for sequential computation. The sovereign does not need to understand quantum mechanics to benefit from quantum speedups; the system dispatches appropriate tasks to quantum hardware transparently.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Nigredo (Available Now)}: Cloud quantum backends. \LogOS{} integrates with cloud quantum APIs (IBM Qiskit Runtime, Amazon Braket, Azure Quantum) through AegisNet-encrypted connections. The sovereign's quantum computation is submitted encrypted where possible (blind quantum computation---see \S\ref{sec:blind-quantum}), executed on the provider's hardware, and results returned encrypted.

 \textbf{Task dispatch}: LogosMentor and the quantum resource manager identify tasks that benefit from quantum execution:
 \begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*., noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Optimisation} (QAOA, VQE): Portfolio optimisation (LogosLedger), route planning, resource scheduling, and supply chain optimisation. Quantum approximate optimisation offers polynomial speedup on NP-hard combinatorial problems.
 \item \textbf{Simulation}: Molecular simulation (drug design, materials science), quantum chemistry, and protein folding. Quantum computers simulate quantum systems exponentially faster than classical computers (Feynman's original motivation).
 \item \textbf{Machine learning}: Quantum kernel methods, quantum neural networks, quantum feature maps. LogosMentor's AI subsystem can train certain models faster using quantum kernels.
 \item \textbf{Search} (Grover's algorithm): Quadratic speedup on unstructured search. Database queries on large datasets, constraint satisfaction, and combinatorial verification.
 \item \textbf{Cryptanalysis}: Sovereign research into cryptographic strength. The sovereign can test their own cryptographic parameters against quantum attack on real quantum hardware.
 \end{enumerate}

 \item \textbf{Albedo (Near-Term)}: Dedicated quantum hardware. Small quantum processing units (QPUs) become available as PCIe cards or network-attached appliances (analogous to the GPU revolution). The sovereign installs a QPU alongside their GPU. LogosKernel manages the QPU as a compute device: job scheduling, memory management, error mitigation.

 LogosLang extends to include quantum types and operations:
 \begin{enumerate}[label=\alph*., noitemsep]
 \item \texttt{qubit} type: represents a quantum bit. Cannot be cloned (the compiler enforces the no-cloning theorem via linear types---a qubit variable can be used exactly once).
 \item \texttt{quantum \{\}} blocks: code regions executed on the QPU. The compiler translates LogosLang quantum expressions into hardware-specific gate sequences.
 \item \texttt{measure} operation: collapses a qubit to a classical bit. The type system tracks which qubits have been measured, preventing use-after-measurement errors.
 \item \texttt{entangle} operation: creates entanglement between qubits. The type system tracks entanglement, ensuring entangled qubits are measured in the correct basis.
 \end{enumerate}

 \item \textbf{Rubedo (Target)}: Sovereign quantum processor. A small ($\sim$100--1,000 logical qubit) error-corrected quantum processor integrated into the sovereign's machine. Fully under the sovereign's physical control. No cloud dependency. No trust in external hardware providers. The sovereign's quantum computations never leave their machine.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Blind Quantum Computation]
\label{sec:blind-quantum}
When using cloud quantum backends (Nigredo), the sovereign faces a trust problem: the cloud provider can see the quantum circuit and the classical inputs. \textbf{Blind quantum computation} (BQC) resolves this: the sovereign encrypts their quantum computation such that the cloud provider executes the computation \textit{without learning what it computes}:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item The sovereign prepares single qubits in random states and sends them to the cloud backend.
 \item The sovereign instructs the backend to perform specific (encrypted) operations on the qubits.
 \item The backend performs the operations without knowing the sovereign's intended computation (the random preparation hides the actual circuit).
 \item The sovereign receives the results and decrypts them locally.
\end{enumerate}

This is the quantum analogue of homomorphic encryption: computation on encrypted data. The cloud provider has the quantum hardware; the sovereign has the algorithm and the results. Neither party has what the other has. BQC is information-theoretically secure---no computational assumption required.
\end{definition}

 \item \textbf{Distributed quantum computation}: Multiple quantum processors connected by quantum links can solve problems that no single processor can handle (analogous to classical distributed computing, but with quantum speedup).
 \item \textbf{Quantum-secured consensus}: Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols using quantum entanglement can achieve consensus with fewer rounds and fewer assumptions than classical BFT.
 \item \textbf{Quantum-anonymous communication}: Quantum protocols can transmit messages with information-theoretic anonymity---not just computational anonymity (like Tor) but provable untraceability guaranteed by physics.

\section{LogosLang Quantum Type System}
\label{sec:quantum-types}

\begin{definition}[Quantum Types in LogosLang]
\label{def:quantum-types}
LogosLang's type system extends to enforce quantum mechanical constraints at compile time:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Linear types for qubits}: A \texttt{qubit} variable has a linear type---it must be used exactly once. This enforces the no-cloning theorem: you cannot copy a qubit, so you cannot use a qubit variable twice. The compiler rejects any program that attempts to clone a quantum state. This eliminates an entire class of quantum programming bugs at compile time.

 \item \textbf{Affine types for measurements}: The \texttt{measure} operation consumes a qubit and produces a classical \texttt{bit}. After measurement, the qubit variable is consumed (cannot be reused). This enforces the irreversibility of quantum measurement.

 \item \textbf{Entanglement tracking}: When two qubits are entangled (via a CNOT gate or similar), the type system records the entanglement. Measuring one entangled qubit automatically constrains the type of the other (it becomes a classically-correlated mixed state, not a free qubit). This prevents the programmer from treating post-measurement entangled qubits as independent.

 \item \textbf{Quantum--classical boundary}: The type system enforces a clear boundary: quantum operations (\texttt{H}, \texttt{CNOT}, \texttt{T}, \texttt{Rz($\theta$)}) operate only on \texttt{qubit} types. Classical operations operate only on \texttt{bit}/\texttt{int}/\texttt{float} types. The \texttt{measure} operation is the only crossing point. This prevents the common bug of accidentally treating a qubit as classical data.

 \item \textbf{Circuit compilation}: LogosLang quantum blocks are compiled to hardware-specific gate sequences via a quantum compiler backend (targeting the sovereign's QPU or a cloud backend's instruction set). The compiler optimises gate count, applies error mitigation strategies, and verifies that the circuit fits within the QPU's qubit count and coherence time.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{The Applied Quantum Operator and Metacursive Closure}

\begin{definition}[Applied Quantum Operator $\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}$]
$\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}$ updates: the QRNG entropy pool (fresh quantum randomness), the QKD key store (distributed keys), the quantum compute job queue (pending and completed quantum tasks), the crypto-agility configuration (current algorithm selections), the quantum network routing table (available QKD links, satellite passes, quantum repeater topology), and the $\varphi$-configuration (QRNG source preference, QKD link policy, quantum compute backend selection, hybrid mode parameters, blind computation settings).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Applied Quantum Metacursive Closure]
\label{thm:applied-quantum-closure}
$\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}(\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}) \equiv \Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}$.

The quantum security system that secures its own quantum security has secured. Specifically: the QRNG generates the random numbers used to key the encryption that protects the QRNG's output channel. The QKD distributes the keys that authenticate the QKD protocol's classical channel. The crypto-agility system uses crypto-agile primitives to protect the crypto-agility configuration. Each quantum subsystem is protected by the quantum security infrastructure that includes itself. Self-application converges because each subsystem operates on finite state (finite entropy pool, finite key store, finite job queue) and self-inclusion adds at most one element to each finite domain.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) QRNG: The QRNG generates random bytes. These bytes key the encryption of the QRNG's USB/PCIe channel. Encrypting the QRNG channel with QRNG-derived keys does not change the QRNG's output (the random bytes are independent of how they are transported). Idempotent. (ii) QKD: The QKD protocol requires an authenticated classical channel. This channel is authenticated using keys from the Autoclave, which may include previous QKD keys. Using QKD keys to authenticate QKD is the standard trusted-relay model. Convergent. (iii) Crypto-agility: The algorithm selection is a finite configuration. Applying crypto-agility to the crypto-agility configuration selects the strongest algorithm for protecting algorithm selections---which is the same strongest algorithm already selected. Fixed point. Product of convergent operators converges. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{Compliance Verification}

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Identity}: $\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A} \equiv \Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}$.
 \item \textbf{Non-Contradiction}: lassical crypto and quantum crypto coexist in hybrid mode.
 \item \textbf{Excluded Middle}: Each sovereign is at exactly one quantum maturity level (Q0--Q5).
 \item \textbf{Tautological Closure}: $\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}(\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}) \equiv \Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}$.
 \item \textbf{Aletheic Alignment}: $T(\mathcal{Q}^A) \equiv R(\mathcal{Q}^A)$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Verdict}: Integrated.

\begin{tautcollapse}{Applied Quantum Sovereignty}
Quantum technologies are not science fiction. They are engineering choices available today. \LogOS{} integrates five quantum technology domains into its sovereign architecture:

\textbf{QRNG}: True quantum randomness for all key generation. Available now for under \$100. Eliminates entropy depletion, state recovery, and seed prediction attacks. The random numbers have no seed, no state, and no algorithm to reverse.

\textbf{Post-quantum cryptography}: ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-65, SLH-DSA---NIST-standardised, lattice-based and hash-based algorithms resistant to Shor's and Grover's. Already deployed as \LogOS{}'s default. Crypto-agility ensures seamless algorithm replacement when the field evolves.

\textbf{QKD}: Information-theoretically secure key distribution. Point-to-point over fibre now; satellite-mediated globally within a decade; quantum-internet at Rubedo. The no-cloning theorem guarantees detection of eavesdroppers.

\textbf{Quantum computation}: Cloud quantum backends now, PCIe QPUs at Albedo, integrated sovereign QPU at Rubedo. Quantum speedups for optimisation, simulation, machine learning, and search. Blind quantum computation ensures the cloud provider cannot see the sovereign's algorithm.

\textbf{Quantum networking}: AegisNet evolves from classical+PQC (Nigredo) through satellite QKD (Albedo) to full quantum internet (Rubedo). Backward-compatible: every sovereign communicates with every other regardless of quantum maturity level.

The progression Q0$\to$Q5 is gradual, additive, and sovereign-controlled. Q0 (post-quantum classical) is secure against all known attacks. Each subsequent level adds defence in depth. No level is mandatory. The sovereign chooses their quantum posture.

$\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}(\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}) \equiv \Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^A}$: the quantum security of quantum security converges.

\section{QRNG Kernel Integration: The Implementation}
\label{sec:qrng-impl}

\begin{definition}[QRNG Kernel Module Architecture]
\label{def:qrng-kernel}
The QRNG integration operates at three levels:

\textbf{Level 1: Hardware Driver.} A Linux kernel module (\texttt{logos\_qrng.ko}) communicates with the USB QRNG device. The module:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item Registers as an \texttt{hwrng} provider via the Linux hardware RNG framework (\texttt{include/linux/hw\_random.h}). This is the standard kernel interface for hardware random number generators---the same interface used by Intel's RDRAND and VirtIO-RNG.
 \item Implements the \texttt{.read} callback: when the kernel requests random bytes, the module reads from the USB device (via USB bulk transfer) and returns raw quantum random data.
 \item Implements health monitoring: continuous statistical testing (NIST SP 800-90B) on the QRNG output stream. If the output fails health tests (indicating device malfunction or tampering), the module deregisters itself and $\Omega$-Vigilance alerts the sovereign: ``QRNG health check failed. Falling back to HRNG.''
 \item Provides a device-specific \texttt{ioctl} interface for LogOS-specific features: entropy rate reporting, device self-test trigger, raw-vs-post-processed mode selection.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Level 2: Entropy Pool Integration.} The \texttt{rngd} daemon (from \texttt{rng-tools}, or the sovereign replacement \texttt{logos-rngd}) continuously reads from \texttt{/dev/hwrng} and feeds quantum random bytes into the kernel's entropy pool (via \texttt{/dev/random} or the \texttt{RNDADDENTROPY} ioctl). The entropy pool mixes QRNG input with other entropy sources (interrupt timing, disk I/O timing, input device timing). The mixing is cryptographic (ChaCha20-based in modern Linux kernels): even if one source is compromised, the others maintain the pool's security. The QRNG is the \textit{primary} source; the others provide defence in depth.

\textbf{Level 3: Autoclave Integration.} The Autoclave (\S\ref{sec:meta-cryptoanalysis}) reads from \texttt{/dev/random} (which is now quantum-seeded) for all key generation operations. No changes to the Autoclave's code are required---it already reads from the system entropy source. The QRNG upgrade is transparent: installing the QRNG device and loading the kernel module automatically upgrades every cryptographic operation in the system from HRNG-quality to QRNG-quality randomness. This is the power of layered architecture: the quantum upgrade propagates through the entire crypto stack without modifying a single line of crypto code.

\textbf{Build procedure (Nigredo):}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., noitemsep]
 \item Kernel module source: \texttt{drivers/char/hw\_random/logos\_qrng.c} (in the LogOS kernel source tree, patched atop the Linux kernel).
 \item Build: \texttt{make -C /lib/modules/\$(uname -r)/build M=\$(pwd) modules}.
 \item Install: \texttt{insmod logos\_qrng.ko} or via \texttt{udev} rule that auto-loads when a supported QRNG device is detected.
 \item Verify: \texttt{cat /sys/devices/virtual/misc/hw\_random/rng\_current} should show \texttt{logos-qrng}. \texttt{rngtest -c 1000 < /dev/hwrng} runs FIPS 140-2 statistical tests.
 \item Integration test: generate 10,000 keys, verify uniform distribution, verify no key reuse, verify entropy estimate $\geq 7.999$ bits per byte (near-perfect entropy).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{Post-Quantum Crypto Integration: The Implementation}
\label{sec:pqc-impl}

\begin{definition}[PQC Integration Architecture]
\label{def:pqc-integration}
Post-quantum cryptography integrates at three points in the \LogOS{} stack:

\textbf{Point 1: The Autoclave Key Generation Pipeline.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item PrimeKey generation uses ML-KEM-1024 for the key encapsulation step: the sovereign's master key pair $(pk, sk)$ is a Kyber-1024 keypair. The public key $pk$ is stored in the $\Gamma$-seal. The secret key $sk$ is derived from the mnemonic constellation via Argon2id and stored only in encrypted memory.
 \item Identity key signing uses ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium): each per-persona identity key is signed by the PrimeKey using a post-quantum signature. The signature is verifiable by anyone with the sovereign's public key.
 \item Backup signing uses SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+): the most conservative algorithm (security relies only on hash function security). Used for long-term archival signatures where the sovereign wants maximum future-proofing.
 \item Implementation: \texttt{liboqs} provides the C implementations. The Autoclave links against \texttt{liboqs} and calls \texttt{OQS\_KEM\_keypair()}, \texttt{OQS\_KEM\_encaps()}, \texttt{OQS\_KEM\_decaps()} for KEM operations; \texttt{OQS\_SIG\_sign()}, \texttt{OQS\_SIG\_verify()} for signatures.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Point 2: HermesGram Message Encryption.}
The Double Ratchet protocol is augmented with post-quantum key exchange:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item Initial key exchange: Hybrid X3DH. Both parties perform a classical X25519 Diffie-Hellman AND a Kyber-1024 KEM encapsulation. The shared secret is: $K = \text{BLAKE3}(K_{\text{X25519}} \| K_{\text{Kyber}})$. This is the root key for the Double Ratchet.
 \item Ratchet steps: Each ratchet step performs a new Kyber-1024 KEM exchange (in addition to the standard X25519 DH ratchet). Forward secrecy is post-quantum: compromising current keys does not reveal past messages even to a quantum adversary.
 \item Implementation: The HermesGram daemon links against both \texttt{libsodium} (for X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305) and \texttt{liboqs} (for Kyber, Dilithium). The hybrid combining function is a BLAKE3 hash of the concatenated shared secrets.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Point 3: AegisNet Transport Encryption.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item TLS 1.3 with hybrid key exchange: Using \texttt{oqs-provider} for OpenSSL, or \texttt{rustls} with the \texttt{pqcrypto} crate, AegisNet's TLS connections negotiate hybrid key exchange (X25519 + ML-KEM-1024). The TLS ClientHello includes both classical and PQ key shares. Servers that support PQ respond with PQ; servers that do not fall back to classical only.
 \item Onion routing: Each layer of the onion uses a separate hybrid KEM. Layer $i$ is encrypted to relay $i$'s public key using X25519 + Kyber. Even if one relay's classical key is later broken by a quantum computer, the PQ key protects the layer.
 \item Certificate authentication: AegisNet node certificates are signed with ML-DSA-65. Certificate chains from the $\Gamma$-seal to the node certificate use post-quantum signatures throughout.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Crypto-Agility Implementation:}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item Every cryptographic operation in \LogOS{} goes through an \texttt{Algorithm Registry}: a runtime-configurable mapping from abstract operations (KEM, Signature, AEAD, Hash, KDF) to concrete implementations. The registry is a LogosLang/Rust \texttt{enum} dispatching to the selected backend.
 \item The $\varphi$-configuration stores the algorithm selection: \texttt{\{kem: "ML-KEM-1024", sig: "ML-DSA-65", aead: "ChaCha20-Poly1305", hash: "BLAKE3", kdf: "Argon2id"\}}.
 \item Hot-swap procedure: (a) Advisory Update delivers new $\varphi$ with updated algorithm. (b) LogosInit reads new $\varphi$, updates Algorithm Registry. (c) New sessions use new algorithm immediately. (d) Background re-encryption daemon re-encrypts stored data incrementally (AletheiaFS blocks re-encrypted during idle I/O, prioritised by sensitivity tag). (e) Old algorithm removed from registry after grace period. (f) $\Omega$-Vigilance confirms: ``Migration to [new algorithm] complete. [old algorithm] retired.''
 \item Testing: The Autological Proof System verifies that the Algorithm Registry's dispatch is exhaustive (every operation has a handler) and that the hot-swap preserves semantic equivalence (data encrypted under old algorithm decrypts identically after re-encryption under new algorithm).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{Quantum Compute Integration: The Implementation}
\label{sec:qc-impl}

\begin{definition}[Quantum Compute Subsystem Architecture]
\label{def:qc-architecture}
The quantum compute subsystem (\texttt{logos-quantum}) is a userspace daemon with three components:

\textbf{Component 1: Backend Abstraction Layer (BAL).}
A uniform API over heterogeneous quantum backends:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \texttt{QuantumBackend} trait (Rust) or interface (LogosLang):
 \begin{itemize}[noitemsep]
 \item \texttt{submit(circuit: QuantumCircuit, shots: u32) -> JobHandle}
 \item \texttt{poll(job: JobHandle) -> JobStatus}
 \item \texttt{result(job: JobHandle) -> MeasurementResult}
 \item \texttt{capabilities() -> BackendCapabilities} (qubit count, gate set, connectivity, error rates)
 \end{itemize}
 \item Implementations: \texttt{IbmBackend} (wraps Qiskit Runtime REST API), \texttt{BraketBackend} (wraps Amazon Braket API), \texttt{LocalSimBackend} (wraps \texttt{qiskit-aer} or \texttt{roqoqo} statevector simulator for testing), \texttt{PcieQpuBackend} (talks to local QPU via PCIe/CXL at Albedo+).
 \item All network communication through AegisNet (encrypted, onion-routed). Cloud providers see encrypted job submissions when blind quantum computation is used.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Component 2: Quantum Circuit Compiler.}
Translates LogosLang quantum blocks into hardware-executable circuits:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Frontend}: Parses LogosLang \texttt{quantum \{\}} blocks. Validates linear types (no-cloning). Tracks entanglement. Verifies measurement semantics. Produces a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) graph.
 \item \textbf{Optimiser}: Gate decomposition (maps abstract gates to the target backend's native gate set), gate cancellation (adjacent inverse gates eliminated), qubit routing (maps logical qubits to physical qubits respecting the backend's connectivity graph), depth minimisation (parallelise independent gates). Uses the \texttt{TKET} optimiser (Cambridge Quantum, open-source) or a sovereign equivalent at Rubedo.
 \item \textbf{Backend}: Emits hardware-specific instructions: OpenQASM 3.0 (IBM), IonQ native gates, Rigetti Quil, or direct control pulses for the local QPU. The QIR abstraction ensures the same LogosLang source compiles to any backend.
 \item \textbf{Error mitigation}: Inserts zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, or readout error correction circuits based on the backend's error model. The sovereign does not need to understand error mitigation; the compiler handles it.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Component 3: Task Dispatcher.}
LogosMentor and the sovereign can submit quantum tasks through two interfaces:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Explicit}: The sovereign writes LogosLang code with \texttt{quantum \{\}} blocks. The compiler compiles, optimises, and submits to the selected backend.
 \item \textbf{Implicit}: LogosMentor identifies classical tasks that would benefit from quantum acceleration. Example: the sovereign asks ``optimise my investment portfolio across these 50 assets.'' LogosMentor recognises this as a combinatorial optimisation problem, formulates it as a QAOA circuit, submits to the quantum backend, and returns results to the sovereign as a classical portfolio allocation. The sovereign sees the answer, not the quantum mechanics.
 \item Task routing policy (configurable via $\varphi$):
 \begin{itemize}[noitemsep]
 \item \texttt{local-first}: Use local QPU if available, fall back to cloud.
 \item \texttt{cloud-first}: Use cloud backends (more qubits, better error rates during Nigredo).
 \item \texttt{simulate-only}: Never submit to real quantum hardware; always simulate locally (for development/testing).
 \item \texttt{blind-required}: Only submit to cloud if blind quantum computation is available for that backend.
 \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Blind Quantum Computation Implementation]
\label{def:bqc-impl}
The Universal Blind Quantum Computation (UBQC) protocol (Broadbent, Fitzsimons, Kashefi 2009) is implemented as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item The sovereign's machine prepares single qubits in states $|+_\theta\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle + e^{i\theta}|1\rangle)$ with randomly chosen $\theta \in \{0, \pi/4, \pi/2, \ldots, 7\pi/4\}$. In Nigredo (no local quantum hardware), this preparation is delegated to a trusted QRNG source: the sovereign generates classical descriptions of the preparation angles using QRNG randomness, and the cloud backend prepares the qubits. True UBQC (with local qubit preparation) requires Albedo-level hardware.
 \item The sovereign instructs the cloud backend to entangle the qubits in a specific graph state (a cluster state for measurement-based quantum computation).
 \item The sovereign sends encrypted measurement instructions: for each qubit, the measurement angle is the ``true'' computation angle PLUS a random offset known only to the sovereign. The cloud backend measures but cannot determine the actual computation (the random offset is information-theoretically hidden).
 \item The sovereign receives the measurement results and subtracts the random offsets to recover the true computation output.
 \item Verification: the sovereign embeds ``trap qubits'' (qubits whose measurement outcome is known in advance). If the cloud backend tampers with the computation, the trap qubits produce incorrect results with detectable probability. The verification is information-theoretic: a dishonest server is detected with probability $1 - (8/9)^t$ where $t$ is the number of trap qubits.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{QKD Integration: The Implementation}
\label{sec:qkd-impl}

\begin{definition}[QKD Engineering Architecture]
\label{def:qkd-engineering}
QKD integration follows the ETSI QKD API standard (ETSI GS QKD 004, 014):

\textbf{Hardware layer}: The QKD device (e.g., ID Quantique Cerberis, Toshiba QKD system, or open-hardware designs) connects to the sovereign's machine via a dedicated Ethernet interface. The device handles the quantum optical layer: photon generation, transmission, detection, and sifting. It exposes a classical API for key retrieval.

\textbf{Key Management Service (KMS) layer}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item The QKD device runs a local KMS that stores quantum-distributed keys in a secure buffer.
 \item The Autoclave queries the KMS via the ETSI QKD API: \texttt{GET /api/v1/keys/\{slave\_SAE\_ID\}/enc\_keys?number=1\&size=256} retrieves a 256-bit QKD key shared with a specific peer.
 \item The Autoclave combines the QKD key with the ML-KEM key and the X25519 key (triple hybrid) via BLAKE3 to produce the session key.
 \item Key lifecycle: QKD keys are single-use. Each key is used for exactly one session key derivation, then deleted from the KMS buffer. This provides perfect forward secrecy: compromising the KMS reveals no past session keys (they have been deleted) and no future session keys (they have not yet been generated by quantum measurement).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{AegisNet integration}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item AegisNet's routing layer maintains a ``QKD capability map'': which peers are reachable via QKD links. The map is updated by the QKD device's link status reports.
 \item When establishing a connection to a QKD-capable peer, AegisNet's key exchange protocol includes a QKD key request step BEFORE the TLS handshake. The QKD key is pre-positioned; the TLS handshake then uses the QKD key as additional keying material (via the TLS \texttt{pre\_shared\_key} extension or a custom KEM that incorporates the QKD key).
 \item Fallback: if the QKD link is down (fibre cut, device malfunction, satellite not in view), the connection proceeds with ML-KEM + X25519 only. The sovereign is notified: ``QKD unavailable for this connection. Using post-quantum classical encryption.''
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Testing}: QKD integration is tested with a loopback configuration: two QKD devices connected by a short fibre spool (1 metre) on the developer's bench. The full key exchange, hybrid combination, and session establishment are exercised without requiring a metropolitan fibre network. A software QKD simulator (\texttt{SimulaQron} or the ETSI reference implementation) provides a testing harness when no QKD hardware is available.
\end{definition}

\section{LogosLang Quantum Type System: The Implementation}
\label{sec:quantum-types-impl}

\begin{definition}[Quantum Types in the Compiler]
\label{def:quantum-types-compiler}
The LogosLang compiler enforces quantum constraints via its type system:

\textbf{Linear types (no-cloning enforcement)}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item A \texttt{Qubit} type is marked as \texttt{linear} in the type system. The compiler's borrow checker (analogous to Rust's, but extended for linearity) ensures each \texttt{Qubit} value is used exactly once: it may be passed to a gate (which consumes it and returns a new \texttt{Qubit}), passed to \texttt{measure} (which consumes it and returns a \texttt{Bit}), or entangled with another qubit (which consumes both and returns an \texttt{EntangledPair}).
 \item Any attempt to use a \texttt{Qubit} twice produces a compile-time error: ``Error: Qubit \texttt{q0} used after consumption. Qubits are linear types (no-cloning theorem). Consider using \texttt{measure} if a classical copy is needed.''
 \item Example (valid):
\begin{verbatim}
 quantum {
 let q0 = qubit::new() // Qubit created
 let q1 = hadamard(q0) // q0 consumed, q1 produced
 let (q2, q3) = cnot(q1, q4) // q1, q4 consumed; q2, q3 produced
 let b0 = measure(q2) // q2 consumed, classical Bit produced
 let b1 = measure(q3) // q3 consumed, classical Bit produced
 }
\end{verbatim}
 \item Example (rejected):
\begin{verbatim}
 quantum {
 let q0 = qubit::new()
 let q1 = hadamard(q0)
 let q2 = hadamard(q0) // ERROR: q0 already consumed
 }
\end{verbatim}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Measurement boundary enforcement}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item Inside a \texttt{quantum \{\}} block, only quantum operations are permitted. Classical operations (\texttt{if}, \texttt{for}, arithmetic) operate only on classical types.
 \item \texttt{measure()} is the only operation that crosses the boundary: it takes a \texttt{Qubit} and returns a \texttt{Bit}. After measurement, the result is classical and can be used freely (copied, compared, stored).
 \item Classical control of quantum operations (``measure a qubit, then conditionally apply a gate to another qubit'') is supported via \texttt{if\_measure}: a special form that measures, branches classically, and applies quantum operations in each branch. The compiler ensures both branches consume the remaining qubits identically (no qubit is consumed in one branch but not the other).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Compilation pipeline}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item LogosLang source $\to$ AST with quantum annotations $\to$ type checking (linearity, measurement, entanglement) $\to$ QIR (Quantum Intermediate Representation) $\to$ optimiser (gate decomposition, routing, cancellation) $\to$ backend emission (OpenQASM 3.0, Quil, native pulses).
 \item The QIR is a directed acyclic graph where nodes are gates and edges are qubit wires. The optimiser transforms this graph while preserving semantic equivalence (verified by the Autological Proof System against a reference statevector simulation for small circuits).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{The Quantum Filesystem: Quantum-Safe Content Addressing}
\label{sec:quantum-fs}

\begin{definition}[Quantum-Safe AletheiaFS]
\label{def:quantum-aletheia}
AletheiaFS (\S\ref{def:distributed-aletheiafs}) uses content-addressing: every block is identified by the hash of its contents ($\text{CID} = \text{BLAKE3}(\text{block})$). BLAKE3 is a 256-bit hash. Grover's algorithm reduces the effective collision resistance from $2^{128}$ to $2^{64}$---still beyond practical attack, but the margin shrinks. For long-term archival integrity (centuries), quantum-safe hashing is prudent:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Hash upgrade path}: AletheiaFS's meta-CID system allows hash algorithm migration. CIDv1 already includes a codec identifier and a multihash prefix that specifies the hash algorithm and digest length. Migrating from BLAKE3-256 to BLAKE3-512 (or a future quantum-safe hash) requires only updating the multihash prefix. Existing CIDs remain valid; new blocks use the new hash; old blocks are re-hashed during background maintenance.
 \item \textbf{Quantum random block keys}: Each AletheiaFS block is encrypted with a unique per-block key. When QRNG is available, per-block keys are derived from quantum random numbers. This eliminates any correlation between block keys that a quantum adversary might exploit.
 \item \textbf{Merkle tree quantum resistance}: AletheiaFS's Merkle trees (for directory integrity and deduplication) use BLAKE3. The tree structure is quantum-resistant because finding a collision in a Merkle tree requires finding a collision in the leaf hash AND propagating it through intermediate nodes---the difficulty compounds multiplicatively. A 256-bit hash in a Merkle tree provides approximately $2^{128}$ quantum collision resistance at the leaf level, multiplied by the tree depth.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{Recognising the Quantum Already Present}
\label{sec:quantum-already}

It IS quantum in its architecture---not because it uses quantum hardware (that is an enhancement, not a requirement) but because its design principles are isomorphic to quantum mechanical principles. The Observation Operator, the Materialisation Cascade, the Potentiality/Actuality formalism, the self-recognition model---all of these are quantum principles expressed in classical code. Adding quantum hardware does not make \LogOS{} quantum. It makes explicit what was already implicit.

\begin{theorem}[The Structural Quantum Theorem]
\label{thm:structural-quantum}
\LogOS{} is structurally isomorphic to a quantum system:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{State space}: The set of all possible system configurations (organ states, data states, session states) forms a state space $\mathcal{H}$ analogous to Hilbert space. Each configuration is a ``basis state.'' The compressed-on-disk state is a superposition; the running state is a collapsed eigenstate.
 \item \textbf{Evolution}: System operations (organ invocation, data processing, mode switching) are transformations on $\mathcal{H}$ analogous to unitary operators. They are reversible (undo/redo), information-preserving (no data loss), and composable (sequential operations compose).
 \item \textbf{Observation}: The sovereign's attention is the measurement operator. It collapses superpositions (invokes organs), determines outcomes (selects modes), and is irreversible in the phenomenological sense (you cannot ``un-see'' a rendered screen, just as you cannot ``un-measure'' a qubit).
 \item \textbf{Entanglement}: Inter-organ communication creates correlations between organ states that persist even when the organs are not directly interacting (e.g., a document edited in LogosWrite and displayed in LogosPresent remains correlated: editing the document updates the presentation).
 \item \textbf{No-cloning}: The sovereign's $\Gamma$-seal (identity) cannot be perfectly copied. This is not merely a design choice but a structural property: the identity is bound to the recognition event (biometric + mnemonic), which is a singular act, not a copyable datum.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The isomorphism is structural, not physical: \LogOS{} does not run on quantum hardware (except at Rubedo). The claim is that the \textit{design principles} are quantum:
(i) State space: finite but exponentially large (combinatorial explosion of organ states $\times$ data states $\times$ session states). Analogous to $2^n$-dimensional Hilbert space for $n$ qubits.
(ii) Evolution: all operations are implemented as deterministic transformations with well-defined inverses (undo histories, transactional filesystem, atomic state changes). Structurally unitary.
(iii) Observation: the Invocation Architecture formalises observation as a state-changing act with irreversible phenomenological consequences. Structurally measurement.
(iv) Entanglement: CRDT-based synchronisation between organs creates non-local correlations that persist independently of direct communication. Structurally entanglement.
(v) No-cloning: the recognition-based identity cannot be separated from the recognition event and therefore cannot be copied without performing the recognition. Structurally no-cloning.
The isomorphism holds component-by-component. $\square$
\end{proof}

\section{The Quantum OS Equation}
\label{sec:quantum-os-equation}

\begin{theorem}[LogOS as Quantum Self-Observation]
\label{thm:logos-quantum}
Composing all quantum aspects:
\[
\boxed{
\text{LogOS} = \mathcal{O}(\mathcal{H}_\Sigma), \quad \mathcal{O} = \exists(\exists), \quad \mathcal{H}_\Sigma = \text{all organ states}
}
\]
\LogOS{} is a quantum system observing itself. The state space $\mathcal{H}_\Sigma$ contains all possible configurations. The observation operator $\mathcal{O} = \exists(\exists)$ is the sovereign's self-recognition mediated by the system. The result $\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{H}_\Sigma)$ is the running OS: a specific configuration collapsed from the space of all possible configurations by the sovereign's attention.

Adding quantum hardware (QRNG, QKD, QPU) does not make \LogOS{} quantum---it already is. Quantum hardware makes the quantum nature \textbf{physically literal}: the QRNG provides truly random collapse events, the QKD provides physics-guaranteed secure entanglement, the QPU executes in actual superposition. The hardware \textit{completes} the architecture; the architecture was always quantum.
\end{theorem}

\section{The Quantum Blueprint Operator and Metacursive Closure}

\label{thm:quantum-blueprint-closure}
$\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^B}(\Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^B}) \equiv \Phi_{\mathcal{Q}^B}$.

The quantum engineering blueprint, applied to itself, yields itself. The QRNG kernel module is compiled by the LogosLang compiler, which uses QRNG-derived randomness for any nondeterministic compilation choices. The PQC library is signed with PQC signatures. The quantum compute subsystem's own configuration is encrypted with the PQC stack. The QKD keys protect the QKD configuration channel. The quantum type system type-checks itself (the compiler is written in LogosLang, which includes quantum types; the compiler's own code is type-checked by the compiler). Each subsystem is built with, protected by, and verified through the quantum infrastructure that includes itself. Self-application converges because each subsystem operates on finite state. $\square$
\end{theorem}

\begin{tautcollapse}{The Quantum Engineering Blueprint}
The previous chapters said \textit{what} and \textit{why}. This chapter says \textit{how}---down to the library names, the kernel module interfaces, the API calls, the build commands, and the test procedures.

QRNG: a Linux kernel module (\texttt{logos\_qrng.ko}) registers as an \texttt{hwrng} provider, feeds quantum random bytes into the entropy pool via \texttt{rngd}, which transparently upgrades every cryptographic operation in the system. \chapter{Sovereign Meta-Backup Architecture:\\MnemosyneVault and the Immortality of Sovereign Data}
\label{sec:meta-backup}

\LogOS{} makes an absolute guarantee: \textbf{no sovereign creation is ever lost.} Every document, website, video, code commit, journal entry, and configuration change is preserved the instant it comes into existence, distributed to multiple independent locations, and recoverable even if the sovereign's primary machine is destroyed, seized, or compromised. The sovereign does not ``remember to back up.'' The system remembers for them.

This chapter specifies MnemosyneVault---the organ of memory---in full engineering detail: the auto-backup engine, the seeding architecture, the granular policy system, the meta-backup (the backup system backing up itself), and the mathematical guarantee that sovereign data survives any single point of failure.

\section{MnemosyneVault: The Organ of Memory}
\label{sec:mnemosyne-full}

\begin{definition}[MnemosyneVault ($\mathfrak{V}$)]
\label{def:mnemosyne-vault}
\textbf{MnemosyneVault} is the sovereign backup, versioning, archival, and distribution organ. It is not a separate ``backup application'' the sovereign must remember to run. It is a \textbf{kernel-integrated daemon} that operates continuously, transparently, and automatically from the moment the system boots until the moment it shuts down. Every file modification in AletheiaFS triggers MnemosyneVault. Every creation event triggers MnemosyneVault. The sovereign's work is preserved before the sovereign finishes their next keystroke.

MnemosyneVault provides seven functions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Continuous versioning}: Every file change is captured as a cryptographically sealed version. Not periodic snapshots---continuous. Every save, every autosave, every atomic write.
 \item \textbf{Instant auto-backup}: Every new creation is immediately copied to at least one backup location (local secondary, encrypted peer, or both) within seconds of creation.
 \item \textbf{Auto-seeding}: New creations are automatically distributed to the sovereign peer network, making them available from multiple independent locations.
 \item \textbf{Granular policy}: The sovereign controls what is backed up, where, how often, to how many locations, and whether auto-seeding is enabled---per file, per directory, per organ, or system-wide.
 \item \textbf{Sealed archival}: Long-term archives are cryptographically sealed, timestamped, and immutable---version chains that cannot be retroactively modified.
 \item \textbf{Disaster recovery}: Complete system state can be restored from any backup location, including bare-metal recovery from a MnemosyneVault archive.
 \item \textbf{Meta-backup}: The backup system backs up itself---its configuration, its version database, its peer list, and its encryption keys are all preserved independently of the data they protect.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{The Auto-Backup Engine}
\label{sec:auto-backup}

\begin{definition}[Creation-Triggered Backup ($\beta_0$)]
\label{def:creation-backup}
The auto-backup engine hooks into AletheiaFS at the VFS (Virtual Filesystem) layer. When any organ writes data---a file save, a database commit, a configuration change, a media export---AletheiaFS emits a \texttt{CHANGE\_EVENT} on the internal event bus (LogosIPC). MnemosyneVault subscribes to all \texttt{CHANGE\_EVENT} messages. The processing pipeline for each event:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Event received}: AletheiaFS reports: file $f$ at path $p$ modified (or created) at time $t$. Content hash (CID) = $h$.
 \item \textbf{Policy lookup}: MnemosyneVault checks the backup policy for $f$ (see \S\ref{sec:backup-policy}). The policy determines: backup tier, number of copies, seeding behaviour, retention period.
 \item \textbf{Delta computation}: If $f$ existed previously, MnemosyneVault computes a binary delta ($\delta_f = f_{\text{new}} \oplus f_{\text{old}}$) using \texttt{zstd} differential compression. Typical delta for a document edit: 0.1--5\% of file size. For a new file: the delta IS the entire file.
 \item \textbf{Version seal}: The delta (or full file for new creations) is encrypted with the sovereign's backup key $K_B$ (derived from the PrimeKey hierarchy), timestamped, and sealed with a $\Gamma$-signature. The sealed version is a \textbf{Version Object} $V = (h_{\text{prev}}, \delta, t, \Gamma_{\text{sig}})$---a chain link in the file's version history.
 \item \textbf{Local write}: The Version Object is written to the local MnemosyneVault store (a dedicated partition or directory in AletheiaFS, separate from the live filesystem). This completes in milliseconds---the file is backed up before the sovereign's application finishes its save animation.
 \item \textbf{Replication dispatch}: Based on the backup policy, the Version Object is queued for replication to one or more remote locations (see \S\ref{sec:backup-locations}).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Latency}: Steps 1--5 complete in $<$50ms for typical files ($<$10MB). The sovereign never waits for backup. The backup is complete before the save confirmation appears in the UI.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Continuous Versioning]
\label{def:continuous-versioning}
Every file in AletheiaFS has a \textbf{version chain}: an ordered sequence of Version Objects $V_0, V_1, V_2, \ldots$ where $V_0$ is the initial creation and each subsequent $V_i$ records the delta from $V_{i-1}$. The chain is a Merkle chain: each Version Object includes the hash of the previous Version Object, forming an immutable, tamper-evident history.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Any version recoverable}: To reconstruct version $V_k$, apply $V_0$ then deltas $\delta_1, \delta_2, \ldots, \delta_k$ sequentially. For efficiency, MnemosyneVault periodically stores \textbf{keyframes} (full snapshots) at configurable intervals (default: every 100 versions or every 24 hours, whichever comes first). Recovery from keyframe $K_j$ requires only deltas $\delta_{j+1}, \ldots, \delta_k$.
 \item \textbf{Version browsing}: The sovereign can browse the version history of any file through LogosVault or any organ's ``Version History'' panel. Visual timeline showing every change, with preview. ``Restore to this version'' is one action.
 \item \textbf{Diff viewing}: Any two versions can be compared side-by-side. For text files: word-level diff. For images: overlay comparison. For structured data: field-level diff. LogosMentor can summarise changes: ``Between version 12 and version 47, you rewrote the introduction, added three citations, and removed the appendix.''
 \item \textbf{Branch and merge}: Sovereigns working collaboratively (via LogosSync) may create divergent version branches. MnemosyneVault tracks branches as parallel Merkle chains. Merge operations are CRDT-based (conflict-free) where possible, with sovereign arbitration for true conflicts.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{Backup Locations: Where Creations Are Preserved}
\label{sec:backup-locations}

\begin{definition}[The Five Backup Tiers]
\label{def:backup-tiers}
MnemosyneVault distributes backups across five independent tiers, each providing a different failure mode:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{clp{5cm}p{3.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Tier} & \textbf{Location} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Protects Against} \\
\midrule
$\tau_0$ & \textbf{Local version store} & Dedicated partition on the same drive. Version Objects written synchronously on every change & Application crash, accidental deletion, file corruption \\
\midrule
$\tau_1$ & \textbf{Local secondary device} & Separate physical drive (second SSD, USB drive, SD card) connected to the same machine. Replicated asynchronously (within seconds) & Primary drive failure, filesystem corruption, hardware fault \\
\midrule
$\tau_2$ & \textbf{Local network peer} & Another sovereign device on the same LAN (desktop $\leftrightarrow$ laptop, or sovereign $\leftrightarrow$ companion). Encrypted, authenticated, real-time sync via LogosSync over LAN & Machine theft, fire, water damage, power surge (same-room disasters) \\
\midrule
$\tau_3$ & \textbf{Remote trusted peer} & A sovereign peer on AegisNet, geographically distant. Encrypted chunks replicated over the encrypted overlay network & House fire, natural disaster, local seizure, jurisdiction-level threat \\
\midrule
$\tau_4$ & \textbf{Cold archival} & Offline medium: USB drive in a safe, M-DISC in a vault, printed QR codes, geographic seed (\S\ref{def:frozen-snapshot}). Updated periodically (weekly/monthly) by the sovereign or on sovereign-defined schedule & Total network destruction, EMP, civilisational collapse, long-term archival (decades to centuries) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Default configuration} (Nigredo): $\tau_0$ is always active (zero configuration). $\tau_1$ activates automatically when a secondary device is detected. $\tau_2$ activates when another sovereign device is on the LAN. $\tau_3$ activates when the sovereign enables AegisNet peering and designates trusted peers. $\tau_4$ is sovereign-initiated (the system reminds but does not force).

\textbf{Minimum safety guarantee}: With $\tau_0$ alone, the sovereign is protected against application-level data loss. With $\tau_0 + \tau_1$, protected against drive failure. With $\tau_0 + \tau_1 + \tau_3$, protected against local disaster. With all five tiers, the sovereign's data survives anything short of global civilisational collapse---and even then, $\tau_4$ on durable media persists.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The Impossibility of Total Data Loss]
\label{thm:no-data-loss}
For a sovereign using $\geq 3$ backup tiers with $\geq 2$ geographically independent locations, the probability of total data loss is:
\[
P(\text{total loss}) = \prod_{i \in \text{tiers}} P(\text{tier } i \text{ fails}) < P(\tau_0) \cdot P(\tau_1) \cdot P(\tau_3)
\]
With realistic failure probabilities (drive failure: $\sim 10^{-2}$/year, house fire: $\sim 10^{-3}$/year, remote peer loss: $\sim 10^{-2}$/year, assuming independence):
\[
P(\text{total loss}) < 10^{-2} \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-2} = 10^{-7}/\text{year}
\]
One in ten million per year. Adding $\tau_4$ (cold archival, failure probability $\sim 10^{-4}$/year for properly stored M-DISC) reduces this to $10^{-11}$/year---effectively impossible within a human lifetime.
\end{theorem}

\section{Auto-Seeding: Immediate Network Distribution}
\label{sec:auto-seeding}

\begin{definition}[Auto-Seeding Engine ($\mathcal{S}$)]
\label{def:auto-seeding}
Auto-seeding extends backup from preservation to \textbf{distribution}: creations are not merely copied to backup locations but made \textbf{available to the sovereign peer network} via AegisNet's distributed filesystem (the IPFS-integrated layer of AletheiaFS). When auto-seeding is enabled for a file or directory:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Creation event}: The sovereign saves a file (document, video, website, code commit).
 \item \textbf{MnemosyneVault backup}: The file is backed up locally and to remote tiers (as above).
 \item \textbf{Seeding}: The file's encrypted content blocks are published to AegisNet's DHT (Distributed Hash Table). Trusted peers who have opted to store seeded content receive the encrypted blocks. The file is now retrievable from any peer that holds a copy.
 \item \textbf{Availability}: If the sovereign's machine goes offline, the file remains available from the peers who seeded it. If the sovereign's machine is seized, the file remains available. If the sovereign's entire local network is destroyed, the file remains available from geographically remote peers.
 \item \textbf{Immediate}: Seeding begins within seconds of creation. By the time the sovereign finishes their next sentence, the previous sentence's backup is distributed across multiple independent nodes.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{The ``compromised? impossible'' guarantee}: When auto-seeding is fully configured, the sovereign's creations exist simultaneously on:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item The sovereign's local machine ($\tau_0$, $\tau_1$).
 \item One or more LAN peers ($\tau_2$).
 \item Multiple remote AegisNet peers ($\tau_3$), each in a different jurisdiction.
 \item Cold archival media ($\tau_4$) in physically separate locations.
\end{enumerate}
An adversary seeking to destroy the sovereign's data must simultaneously compromise ALL of these locations---which requires simultaneous physical access to multiple jurisdictions, penetration of AegisNet's onion-routed encryption, AND discovery of cold storage locations. This is, for practical purposes, impossible.

\textbf{Encryption throughout}: Every seeded block is encrypted with the sovereign's backup key $K_B$ before leaving the sovereign's machine. Peers store opaque ciphertext. No peer can read the sovereign's data. Even if every peer is compromised, the adversary obtains only encrypted blocks that are computationally (and with QKD, information-theoretically) indistinguishable from random noise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Erasure-Coded Seeding]
\label{def:erasure-seeding}
For maximum resilience, auto-seeding uses \textbf{erasure coding} (Reed-Solomon or fountain codes): a file of $k$ blocks is encoded into $n > k$ blocks such that \textit{any} $k$ of the $n$ blocks suffice to reconstruct the original file. The sovereign configures the redundancy factor $r = n/k$:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item $r = 2$ (default): File encoded into $2k$ blocks. Any $k$ blocks reconstruct. Half the peers can disappear and the file is still recoverable.
 \item $r = 3$ (high resilience): File encoded into $3k$ blocks. Two-thirds of peers can disappear.
 \item $r = 5$ (maximum): File encoded into $5k$ blocks. 80\% of peers can vanish simultaneously.
\end{enumerate}

Erasure coding is more storage-efficient than simple replication: storing 2 copies ($r=2$) via replication requires $2\times$ the space on a single peer; storing $r=2$ via erasure coding distributes the overhead across many peers, with each peer storing only $1/k$-th of the total overhead. The sovereign's data is more resilient with LESS total storage consumed.
\end{definition}

\section{The Sovereign Backup Policy System}
\label{sec:backup-policy}

\begin{definition}[Backup Policies ($\mathcal{P}_B$)]
\label{def:backup-policies}
The sovereign has \textbf{total control} over what is backed up, where, how often, and how many copies exist. Policies are defined at four granularity levels:

\textbf{Level 1: System-wide defaults.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{Auto-backup}: ON by default. Every file change is backed up to $\tau_0$ (local version store). The sovereign can turn this OFF (not recommended; $\Omega$-Vigilance warns).
 \item \textbf{Auto-seeding}: OFF by default (privacy-first). The sovereign enables auto-seeding explicitly and selects trusted peers. When enabled, applies to all files unless overridden at a lower level.
 \item \textbf{Retention period}: How long old versions are kept. Default: indefinite (all versions kept forever). The sovereign can set: 30 days, 90 days, 1 year, 5 years, or forever. Old versions beyond the retention period are pruned from $\tau_0$ and $\tau_1$ (but NOT from $\tau_3$/$\tau_4$ if the sovereign has configured archival retention separately).
 \item \textbf{Redundancy factor}: Default $r = 2$ for seeded files. Configurable per the sovereign's risk tolerance and peer count.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Level 2: Per-organ policies.}
Each organ can have its own backup policy:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \texttt{LogosWrite}: All documents auto-backed up to $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$, $\tau_3$. Continuous versioning with keyframes every 50 edits. Auto-seeding optional.
 \item \texttt{LogosCode}: All repositories auto-backed up. Each commit is a Version Object. Auto-seeding enabled for public repositories, disabled for private.
 \item \texttt{LogosCut}/\texttt{LogosForge}: Media projects auto-backed up to $\tau_0$. Large files ($>$1GB) backed up to $\tau_1$ only on export (to avoid filling the version store with intermediate renders). Final exports auto-seeded if the sovereign enables public distribution.
 \item \texttt{LogosJournal}: Maximum backup. Auto-backed up to $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$, $\tau_3$ immediately. Auto-seeding DISABLED by default (private journal). Retention: forever.
 \item \texttt{EchoCrypt}: Message history backed up to $\tau_0$ and $\tau_1$. NOT auto-seeded (private communications). Burn-capable messages excluded from backup entirely.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Level 3: Per-directory policies.}
The sovereign can set policies on any directory:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item ``My Projects'': $\tau_0 + \tau_1 + \tau_3$, auto-seeding ON, $r = 3$.
 \item ``Temporary'': $\tau_0$ only, retention 7 days, no seeding.
 \item ``Published Works'': $\tau_0 + \tau_1 + \tau_3 + \tau_4$, auto-seeding ON with $r = 5$, retention forever.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Level 4: Per-file policies.}
Any file can have an individual policy that overrides all higher levels:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item ``This file is extremely sensitive'': $\tau_0 + \tau_1$ only, NO seeding, NO remote peers, retention forever.
 \item ``This file should be everywhere'': all tiers, $r = 5$, auto-seeded to all peers.
 \item ``Do not back up this file'': backup disabled entirely (the sovereign accepts the risk; $\Omega$-Vigilance notes the exception).
\end{enumerate}

Policy inheritance: Level 4 overrides Level 3 overrides Level 2 overrides Level 1. If no policy is set at a given level, the next higher level's policy applies. If no policy is set anywhere, the system-wide default applies.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The Policy Configuration Interface]
\label{def:policy-interface}
The sovereign configures backup policies through three interfaces:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), noitemsep]
 \item \textbf{LogosConfig} $\to$ \textbf{Backup}: System-wide and per-organ defaults. Visual dashboard showing: total backup size, number of versions stored, peer health, last backup time, and any warnings (e.g., ``secondary drive not connected for 7 days'').
 \item \textbf{Right-click $\to$ Backup Policy}: In LogosVault or any file browser, right-click any file or directory to view/edit its backup policy. One-click presets: ``Maximum safety,'' ``Standard,'' ``Local only,'' ``No backup.''
 \item \textbf{LogosMentor}: ``Back up everything I create to three peers.'' ``Stop seeding my journal.'' ``Show me what's not backed up.'' ``How safe is my data right now?'' Natural language configuration, translated to policy rules by LogosMentor and confirmed by the sovereign before applying.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\section{Auto-Backup Triggers: What Gets Backed Up and When}
\label{sec:backup-triggers}

\begin{definition}[Trigger Types]
\label{def:trigger-types}
MnemosyneVault responds to eight categories of events:

\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{clp{5.5cm}p{3cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{ID} & \textbf{Trigger} & \textbf{Description} & \textbf{Default Action} \\
\midrule
$\beta_0$ & \textbf{File save} & Any organ saves a file (explicit save, autosave, export) & Immediate: $\tau_0$. Async: $\tau_1$, $\tau_3$ \\
$\beta_1$ & \textbf{File creation} & A new file is created for the first time & Immediate: $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$. Async: $\tau_3$, seed \\
$\beta_2$ & \textbf{Commit} & LogosCode repository commit & Immediate: $\tau_0$. Push to $\tau_3$ (as git remote) \\
$\beta_3$ & \textbf{Publish} & LogosStream/LogosPublish/website publish & Immediate: all tiers. Auto-seed with $r \geq 3$ \\
$\beta_4$ & \textbf{Configuration change} & Any $\varphi$-configuration modified & Immediate: $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$. $\Gamma$-sealed snapshot \\
$\beta_5$ & \textbf{Key event} & Key generation, rotation, or revocation in the Autoclave & Immediate: $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$, encrypted to $\tau_4$ \\
$\beta_6$ & \textbf{Scheduled snapshot} & Periodic full-system snapshot (default: daily) & Full system image to $\tau_1$. Delta to $\tau_3$ \\
